card.headline: Alert ears, bright eyes, steady eating
card.look: A healthy donkey stands alert with ears moving towards sounds, eyes bright and clear, and spends much of the day slowly picking at fibrous feed. It passes firm, round droppings and walks evenly on upright, well-shaped hooves.
card.action: Learn your donkey's normal temperature, appetite, droppings and behaviour now, so you notice the small changes early, because donkeys hide pain.

detail.summary: This page describes what a normal, healthy donkey looks, sounds and behaves like, so you can spot trouble early. Donkeys are stoic, meaning they hide pain and illness far better than horses or cattle. By the time a donkey looks obviously sick, the problem is often serious. Knowing your own donkey's normal habits is the most useful tool you have.
detail.cause: Good health in a donkey comes from a few simple things working together. Donkeys evolved in dry, harsh lands eating tough, low-energy plants, so their gut works best on plenty of fibre, such as straw, dry grass and browse, eaten slowly through the day. Too much rich feed, lush wet-season grass, maize bran or sugary food makes them fat, and fat donkeys are at risk of laminitis (painful inflammation inside the hoof) and hyperlipaemia (a dangerous build-up of fat in the blood that can follow even a short period of not eating). Clean water at all times keeps the gut moving and prevents impaction colic, a blockage of the bowel. A donkey's coat is not waterproof like a horse's, so shelter from rain and cold wind, especially in the long rains, keeps it warm and stops skin and foot problems. Healthy feet need regular trimming and dry standing ground. Healthy teeth let the donkey chew fibre properly. Control of worms, ticks and flies, protection against tetanus, fair workloads, a well-fitted harness and a companion donkey all keep the body and mind strong. When any of these slips, the donkey usually copes quietly for a while, which is why small changes in its behaviour matter.
spread: Most donkey health problems are triggered by management rather than spread, so watch for changes in feed, water, work and weather.
A sudden change of diet, such as moving onto lush grass after the rains or adding concentrates, can upset the gut and trigger colic or laminitis.
Not eating for even a day or two, from stress, pain, bad teeth, transport or losing a companion, can trigger hyperlipaemia, especially in fat donkeys, pregnant jennies and older animals.
Standing in mud and wet bedding during the long and short rains softens hooves and allows thrush and other foot infections.
Contact with new or untreated donkeys at markets, water points and shared grazing can bring in worms, lice, mange mites, ringworm and infectious diseases.
Heavy loads, long hours in the heat and poor harness fit cause dehydration, exhaustion and wounds that can become infected, including with tetanus.
In tsetse areas, fly bites can pass on trypanosomosis, and ticks and biting flies can carry other blood infections.
detail.atRisk: Every donkey benefits from regular checks, but some need closer watching. Working donkeys pulling water carts, carrying goods or ploughing face heat stress, dehydration, harness sores and overwork, especially in the hot dry months. Fat donkeys, older donkeys, pregnant and nursing jennies (female donkeys) and miniature breeds have the highest risk of hyperlipaemia when they stop eating. Old donkeys often have worn or loose teeth and lose condition. Foals need colostrum (first milk) in their first hours and careful worm control. Donkeys kept alone, recently moved or recently bereaved of a companion are stressed and may eat less. In pastoral and free-range systems, donkeys may go without close daily checks for days, so problems can be missed. During the long rains, wet ground and cold nights raise the risk of foot and chest problems, while green flushes of grass raise the risk of laminitis.

early: Temperature between 36.5 and 37.8 °C taken in the rectum, slightly higher after work or on a very hot afternoon.
Heart rate (pulse) of roughly 36 to 68 beats per minute and breathing of roughly 12 to 28 breaths per minute at rest, with quiet, even breaths.
Bright, clear eyes with no discharge, and ears that move and turn towards sounds, people and other animals.
Steady interest in food, picking at forage for many hours of the day, and drinking clean water, though donkeys often drink less than horses and may prefer it not too cold.
Plenty of firm, round, fairly dry dung balls passed through the day, and pale yellow urine passed without straining.
Gurgling gut sounds on both sides of the belly when you put your ear against the flank.
Pink, moist gums, and a clean nose with no thick discharge or bad smell.
Even, sound walking on all four legs, with upright, U-shaped hooves that are trimmed, free of cracks and not overgrown.
A body condition score of about 3 on a 1 to 5 scale: you can feel the ribs and backbone with light pressure but not see them sharply, and the neck and rump are not bulging with hard fat.
Normal social behaviour: grooming its companion, braying, rolling in dust, dozing standing up and lying down for short rests.
advanced: Eating less, eating slowly, sorting feed or ignoring treats it usually loves. In a donkey this is an emergency, not something to watch for days.
Standing quietly at the back of the shelter, head low, ears drooping or held back, not interested in people or its companion. Dullness is often the only sign of serious pain.
Fewer or smaller dung balls, very dry dung, diarrhoea, or no dung at all for several hours.
Temperature above 37.8 °C or below 36.5 °C at rest, or a pulse above about 68 beats per minute at rest.
Pawing, looking at the belly, repeated lying down and getting up, or lying flat for long periods, which can mean colic.
Shifting weight, leaning back onto the heels, reluctance to walk, or heat in the hooves, which can mean laminitis.
Dropping balls of half-chewed food from the mouth (called quidding), drooling, a bad smell from the mouth or swelling of the face, which point to tooth problems.
Coughing, nasal discharge, fast breathing, swellings under the jaw, skin sores, hair loss, or harness wounds that are not healing.

lookalikes.name: Dust rolling versus colic rolling
lookalikes.howToTell: Healthy donkeys roll in dust to scratch and protect their skin, then get up, shake and go back to eating. A donkey with colic rolls repeatedly, lies down and gets up, looks at its belly, stops eating and passes less dung. If in doubt, take the temperature and pulse and call the vet.

lookalikes.name: Resting a hind leg versus lameness
lookalikes.howToTell: Dozing donkeys often rest one hind leg with the hoof tipped, and swap legs from time to time. A lame donkey limps when walking, shifts weight constantly, rests a front leg, or refuses to put a foot down. Walk the donkey on hard, flat ground and watch the head and hips.

lookalikes.name: Calm, quiet nature versus dullness
lookalikes.howToTell: Donkeys are naturally calmer and slower than horses, but a healthy donkey still watches you, moves its ears and shows interest in food. A sick donkey stands apart, head low, ears floppy, and does not respond as usual. Compare with how your donkey normally behaves.

lookalikes.name: Fat neck crest or big belly versus good condition or pregnancy
lookalikes.howToTell: Many farmers think a round donkey is a healthy one, but hard fat on the neck, rump and shoulders means the donkey is overweight and at risk of laminitis and hyperlipaemia. A big belly can be fat, worms, gut fill or pregnancy. Feel the ribs and backbone, and ask the vet if you suspect a jenny is in foal.

detail.diagnosis: A home health check takes about ten minutes and is best done weekly when the donkey is calm and rested, plus any time it seems off. Write the results in a notebook so you know your donkey's own normal. First, stand back and watch: is it eating, alert, standing evenly, breathing quietly? Check the droppings and bedding. To take the temperature, use a digital thermometer lubricated with a little petroleum jelly. Tie the donkey or have a helper hold it, stand beside the hindquarters, not directly behind, lift the tail and gently insert the thermometer into the rectum, tilted slightly so the tip touches the wall. Hold it until it beeps, read it, then clean and disinfect it. For the pulse, place two fingers under the jaw bone where an artery crosses, or put your hand on the left chest just behind the elbow, count the beats for 30 seconds and double it. Count breathing by watching the flank rise and fall for one minute. Put your ear on each side of the belly to listen for gut gurgles. Lift the lip: gums should be pink and moist, and if you press with a thumb the colour should return within about two seconds. Run your hands over the whole body to feel for heat, swellings, sores, ticks or pain, especially under the harness. Pick up each foot to check for stones, cracks, bad smells and overgrowth. Score body condition by feeling the neck, ribs, back and rump. A weigh tape made for donkeys, or a height-and-girth chart, helps track weight over time. If anything is outside normal, give the vet your notes, what the donkey has eaten, when it last passed dung and any recent changes.
firstSteps: If your donkey is off its food or dull, treat it as urgent and call the vet or County Veterinary Officer the same day rather than waiting to see.
Take and write down the temperature, pulse, breathing and when the donkey last ate, drank and passed dung, so the vet has clear information.
Stop all work, remove the harness or load, and move the donkey to a quiet, shaded, dry place with its companion nearby.
Offer clean fresh water and its usual fibrous feed, such as hay or straw, but do not force-feed or give large amounts of concentrates.
Keep the donkey out of rain and cold wind, and if it is cold or wet, dry it gently and cover it with a dry sack or blanket.
Separate a donkey with coughing, nasal discharge, skin disease or diarrhoea from others, and wash your hands and tools after handling it.
Do not give any medicines, including pain killers or dewormers, without a vet's advice, as some drugs can hide signs or be unsafe for donkeys.
Handle the donkey calmly and safely, standing to the side and avoiding the back legs, especially if it is in pain.
detail.vetTreatment: Routine vet care keeps a healthy donkey healthy and is much cheaper than treating illness. A vet or trained animal health worker can carry out a yearly health check covering teeth, heart, lungs, feet, skin, weight and body condition. Tetanus vaccination is strongly recommended for all donkeys, as wounds from harness, thorns and hooves are common; the vet will advise on the starting course and boosters. In some areas the vet may advise rabies vaccination or other vaccines depending on local disease risks. Teeth should be checked at least once a year, with sharp edges filed (called rasping or floating) so the donkey can chew fibre. Worm control works best when guided by the vet, ideally using dung tests called faecal egg counts to decide which donkeys need treatment and with which drug class, rather than deworming everyone blindly, as overuse leads to worms that resist the medicine. Tick, lice and mange control products should also be chosen with the vet, as not all livestock products are safe or licensed for donkeys. Hoof trimming by a trained person every six to ten weeks or as needed keeps feet healthy. In tsetse areas the vet may discuss trypanosomosis prevention. Any medicine must be prescribed by a vet, and donkeys may need different drugs or doses from horses because their bodies process some medicines differently. If donkey milk or meat is used, ask about withdrawal periods, the time after treatment before milk or meat is safe.
prevention: Feed a high-fibre diet based on straw, dry grass or hay and browse, with limited lush grass, and avoid sugary feeds, bread and large amounts of maize bran or dairy meal.
Provide clean water at all times, and check water points daily, especially on hot days and after work, since dehydration can lead to impaction colic.
Give dry, draught-free shelter with a solid roof, because a donkey's coat soaks through in rain; this is vital in the long and short rains and on cold highland nights.
Keep standing areas and bedding dry and clean, and pick out feet regularly to prevent thrush and other hoof problems.
Arrange hoof trimming every six to ten weeks and dental checks at least yearly, and never leave overgrown or cracked hooves.
Vaccinate against tetanus, and follow a vet-guided plan for worms, ticks, lice and flies.
Check body condition every two weeks and adjust feed and exercise to keep the score near 3, avoiding both thinness and obesity.
Keep donkeys in pairs or groups where possible, limit loads to a fair weight for the donkey's size, rest working donkeys in shade with water, and use well-fitted, padded harnesses.
detail.impact: For many Kenyan households, a donkey is a working partner that carries water, firewood, produce and building materials, ploughs land and earns cash through cart transport. When a donkey falls sick, the family may lose hours each day fetching water by hand and lose income from hired transport. Serious illnesses such as colic, hyperlipaemia, laminitis and tetanus can be expensive to treat and are often fatal if caught late. Because donkeys hide illness, the cost of missing early signs is high. A few minutes each week checking temperature, appetite, droppings, feet and condition, plus basic routine care, protects a valuable asset and allows the donkey to work well for many years. Donkeys are also at risk of theft in some areas, so keeping them close, well-handled and recorded helps protect them.
detail.humanHealth: A healthy, well-cared-for donkey poses little disease risk to people, but some donkey infections can pass to humans. Ringworm, a fungal skin infection showing as round hairless patches, spreads by touch, so wear gloves and wash hands after handling affected skin. Rabies is a fatal risk anywhere in Kenya: never put your hand in the mouth of a donkey that is drooling, behaving strangely or cannot swallow, and report any animal bite to a health facility at once. Wounds from donkey kicks, bites or dirty hooves can lead to tetanus in people, so keep your own tetanus vaccination up to date. Always wash hands after handling donkeys, dung and thermometers, especially before eating.
detail.outlook: A donkey that is fed mainly fibre, watered well, sheltered from rain, kept at a healthy weight and checked regularly can live and work for 25 to 30 years or more. Most serious donkey illnesses have a much better chance of recovery when they are noticed early, often from nothing more than a small drop in appetite, quieter behaviour or fewer droppings. The outlook gets worse the longer a problem goes unnoticed, especially in fat, old, pregnant or stressed donkeys. Farmers who know their donkey's normal temperature, habits and body condition, and who call the vet quickly when something changes, give their animals the best chance.

faqs.q: My donkey looks fine but has eaten less today. Should I wait?
faqs.a: No. In donkeys, eating less is one of the most important warning signs. Donkeys hide pain, and a donkey that stops eating, especially if it is fat, old, pregnant or stressed, can quickly develop hyperlipaemia, a dangerous fat build-up in the blood. Take the temperature, check the droppings and call the vet the same day. Keep offering water and its usual forage while you wait.

faqs.q: Is a fat, round donkey a healthy donkey?
faqs.a: Not usually. Many donkeys in Kenya are either too thin from hard work or too fat from rich grass and bran. Hard fat on the neck crest, shoulders and rump raises the risk of laminitis and hyperlipaemia. Aim for a score of about 3 on a 1 to 5 scale, where you can feel the ribs easily under a thin layer of fat but cannot see them sharply. Note that neck fat can stay hard even after weight loss, so feel the whole body.

faqs.q: Can I use my horse or cattle temperature and pulse figures for my donkey?
faqs.a: Use donkey figures instead. A healthy donkey's rectal temperature is about 36.5 to 37.8 °C, pulse about 36 to 68 beats per minute and breathing about 12 to 28 breaths per minute at rest. Each donkey has its own normal within these ranges, so take readings when it is healthy and calm and write them down to compare later.

faqs.q: Why does my donkey need a shelter when it lives in dry country?
faqs.a: Donkeys handle heat and dryness well, but their coat is not waterproof like a horse's. In the long and short rains a donkey can get soaked to the skin, become chilled and develop chest, skin and hoof problems. Shade is also important in hot, dry months. A simple roofed shelter with a dry floor where the donkey can choose to go makes a big difference.

faqs.q: How often should I deworm and trim my donkey?
faqs.a: There is no single rule for every farm. Many donkeys need hooves trimmed every six to ten weeks, but this depends on ground and wear. For worms, the best approach is a vet-guided plan using dung tests, because deworming too often or with the wrong product encourages worms that resist the medicine. Ask your vet or County Veterinary Officer to help set a plan for your area and season.

faqs.q: Is it normal for my donkey to lie down or roll?
faqs.a: Yes, healthy donkeys lie down for short rests, often in the sun, and roll in dust to scratch and care for their coat. It becomes a concern if the donkey lies down and gets up repeatedly, rolls again and again, looks at its belly, refuses food, sweats or lies flat for long periods. Those are signs of colic or other pain and need a vet quickly.

products.role: An oral rehydration and heat-stress relief solution that can be offered alongside plenty of clean water to working donkeys after long, hot days or journeys, helping replace water and salts lost through effort. It supports a healthy donkey's comfort and recovery from work; it does not replace shade, rest, fair workloads or a vet visit if the donkey is dull or off its food.

healthy.imagePrompt: A healthy grey East African donkey standing alert in a dry, sunny Kenyan smallholding yard, ears upright and turned forward, bright eyes, good body condition, neatly trimmed upright hooves, calmly eating straw beside a simple roofed shelter and a water trough.
healthy.seoDescription: Know what a healthy donkey looks like: normal temperature, pulse, droppings, hooves, ears and body condition, plus early warning signs for Kenyan farmers.

card.headline: Dull donkey, not eating, no droppings
card.look: The donkey stands quietly with its head low, ignores food, lies down more than usual and passes few or no droppings; some will look round at their belly, paw the ground or roll. Donkeys hide pain, so a quiet, 'off' donkey may be in serious trouble.
card.action: Remove all feed, keep the donkey calm in a safe shaded place with water available, and call a vet straight away, because colic in donkeys is an emergency.

detail.summary: Colic means pain in the abdomen (belly). In donkeys it is most often caused by a blockage of dry food in the gut (impaction), gas, sand, sudden feed changes, worn or broken teeth, or worms. Donkeys are very stoic: they show pain quietly, often just by being dull and not eating, so colic is easy to miss until it is advanced. Colic can kill, and a donkey that stops eating for even a short time can also develop hyperlipaemia, a dangerous fat-in-the-blood condition, so every case needs a vet quickly.
detail.cause: Colic is a sign, not a single disease. The donkey's gut is long and folded, with narrow bends where dry, coarse food can pack together and block the passage. The most common cause in East African donkeys is impaction: a hard plug of poorly chewed fibre such as dry grass, maize stover, straw or wheat husks, made worse when the donkey is not drinking enough. Bad teeth (sharp edges, missing, loose or overgrown teeth, common in older working donkeys) mean food is swallowed in long pieces that are hard to digest. Sand and soil eaten while grazing on bare ground or from feed thrown on the floor can settle in the gut and irritate or block it. Gas colic happens when food ferments too fast, for example after a sudden switch to lush wet-season grass, too much grain, maize bran or kitchen waste. Worms, especially large and small strongyles (redworms) and in young donkeys roundworms, damage the gut wall and blood supply, and tapeworms can trigger blockages where the small and large intestine meet. In Kenyan towns, donkeys often eat plastic bags, ropes and rubbish, which can form a mass that blocks the gut. Less often, a section of gut twists or becomes trapped, cutting off its blood supply; this is very painful and usually fatal without surgery. Whatever the cause, a blocked or stretched gut causes pain, stops normal movement of food, pulls fluid out of the body and can let toxins into the blood. A donkey in pain stops eating, and in donkeys this quickly mobilises body fat into the blood (hyperlipaemia), which can damage the liver and kidneys.
spread: Colic is not infectious and does not spread from donkey to donkey, but several donkeys on the same farm can develop it if they share the same poor feed, water or worm burden.

Not drinking enough water is a major trigger, for example when water is far away, dirty, too cold in the early morning in highland areas, or when working donkeys are not given time to drink during long carting days.
Sudden changes in diet, such as moving from dry-season stover to lush green grass after the rains, or suddenly being given grain, maize bran, bread or kitchen leftovers, can upset the gut.
Feeding only very coarse, dry roughage such as straw or stover, especially to donkeys with poor teeth, increases the risk of impaction.
Grazing on bare, sandy or overgrazed land, or eating feed thrown on the ground, leads to sand and soil building up in the gut.
Heavy worm burdens from irregular or no deworming, and grazing on the same small paddock year after year, damage the gut.
Eating plastic bags, sacks, ropes and rubbish, common for donkeys roaming in towns and markets, can cause blockages.
Stress from overwork, long transport, sudden confinement, pain elsewhere, or a change of owner or companion can reduce eating and drinking and set off colic.
detail.atRisk: Any donkey can get colic, but some are at higher risk. Older donkeys with worn, loose or missing teeth are very prone to impaction. Working donkeys used for carting water, sand, building materials or farm produce are at risk when they are overworked, dehydrated and fed irregularly on poor roughage. Donkeys that are suddenly confined, for example moved from free-ranging to a small boma, or that have reduced exercise because of lameness, are more likely to impact. Young foals with heavy roundworm burdens and donkeys that have not been dewormed are at risk of worm-related colic. Urban and peri-urban donkeys that scavenge rubbish are at risk of plastic blockages. Risk rises in the dry season when grazing is coarse and water is scarce, in cold highland mornings when donkeys drink less, and at the start of the long and short rains when lush grass appears suddenly. Fat donkeys, pregnant or nursing jennies (females), miniature donkeys and stressed donkeys are at especially high risk of hyperlipaemia if colic stops them eating.

early: Dullness and depression: the donkey stands quietly in a corner with its head low, ears back or drooping, and seems less interested in its surroundings or companions.
Reduced appetite or complete refusal of feed, including favourite feeds; a donkey that does not finish its food should always be checked.
Fewer droppings than normal, or droppings that are small, dry, hard or coated in mucus (slime).
Lying down more than usual, or lying down at an unusual time of day, and being reluctant to get up.
Looking round at the flank or belly, lifting the upper lip, grinding the teeth or stretching out as if to urinate without passing much urine.
Shifting weight, resting legs repeatedly or standing in an odd, tense posture.
Quieter or fewer gut sounds when you put your ear against the flank; a healthy gut gurgles regularly.
advanced: Pawing the ground, kicking at the belly, getting up and lying down repeatedly, or rolling, though many donkeys never show these dramatic signs even when very sick.
No droppings at all for many hours and a completely silent belly when you listen at both flanks.
Fast breathing and sweating, sometimes patchy, even at rest in the shade.
Gums that are dark red, purple or muddy grey instead of moist pink, and that are dry or tacky to touch.
A swollen, tight belly, especially with gas colic.
Weakness, wobbliness, cold ears and legs, or collapse.
Signs that hyperlipaemia is developing: deep depression, total refusal to eat, bad breath, a yellowish tinge to the gums or eyes, and swelling under the belly or head.

lookalikes.name: Hyperlipaemia (fat mobilisation)
lookalikes.howToTell: Hyperlipaemia also makes a donkey dull and stop eating, and it often follows colic or any stress. Colic usually comes with reduced droppings and belly-focused signs such as looking at the flank or lying down; hyperlipaemia tends to show deep, steady depression, yellowish gums and sometimes swelling, often in fat or pregnant donkeys. They often occur together, and only a vet's blood test can confirm hyperlipaemia.

lookalikes.name: Laminitis (founder)
lookalikes.howToTell: Laminitis is painful inflammation inside the hooves, often after grain overload or lush grass. The donkey may lie down a lot and seem in pain like colic, but it stands leaning back to take weight off the front feet, is reluctant to walk, and the hooves feel hot with a strong pulse above the hoof. Droppings are usually normal.

lookalikes.name: Choke (blocked food pipe)
lookalikes.howToTell: In choke, food is stuck in the oesophagus (food pipe) in the neck. The donkey is distressed, stretches its neck, coughs or gags, and food, saliva or green fluid comes out of the nose and mouth. Colic does not usually cause food coming from the nose.

lookalikes.name: Urinary blockage, foaling or uterine problems
lookalikes.howToTell: A donkey that strains repeatedly and passes little or no urine may have bladder stones or a urinary problem. A heavily pregnant jenny that is restless, lying down and looking at her flank may be starting to foal or have a twisted uterus. A vet examination is needed to tell these apart from gut colic.

detail.diagnosis: A vet diagnoses colic by examining the whole donkey. They will check the heart rate, breathing rate, temperature, gum colour, how quickly colour returns to the gum after pressing it, and listen to the gut sounds on both sides. They look at the teeth and droppings. Where the donkey is large enough, the vet may do a rectal examination, gently feeling inside through the back passage to find an impaction, gas or a twisted gut, although this is more limited in small donkeys. They may pass a stomach tube through the nose to release gas or fluid and check for reflux (fluid backing up from the gut), which can indicate a serious blockage. A blood test, especially for triglycerides (blood fats), is very important in donkeys to check for hyperlipaemia, and may also check dehydration, liver and kidney function. Some referral clinics can use ultrasound. If a donkey dies, a post-mortem can show the cause and protect the rest of the herd. To help the vet, note when you last saw the donkey eat, drink and pass droppings, what it has been fed and any recent changes, when it was last dewormed and with what, how much work it has done, whether it is pregnant, and any changes in signs over time. Keep a sample of recent droppings and the feed if you can.
firstSteps: Call a vet immediately; colic in donkeys is an emergency and early treatment greatly improves the chance of survival. If you cannot reach a private vet, contact your County Veterinary Office, an animal welfare organisation or a local agrovet who can link you to a vet.
Remove all feed, including hay and bedding the donkey might eat, until the vet has examined it, but leave clean, fresh water available and note whether it drinks.
Put the donkey in a safe, shaded, well-bedded area with soft ground and no sharp objects or ditches, so that if it lies down or rolls it will not injure itself.

Let a quiet donkey lie down and rest; you do not need to force it to walk for hours. If it is rolling violently, gently lead it on a short walk only if you can do so safely, and keep yourself out of reach of its legs.
Keep its usual companion donkey close by, within sight, because donkeys bond strongly and separation stress can make things worse.
Stop all work immediately and remove any harness, saddle or cart.

Check and write down simple information while you wait: whether droppings are passed, gut sounds at both flanks, gum colour, behaviour every 15 to 30 minutes, and anything unusual it may have eaten such as plastic.
Do not give any medicine, painkiller, oil, traditional remedy or drench by mouth before the vet arrives; drenching can go into the lungs, and painkillers can hide signs the vet needs to see.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on the cause and how severe it is, and must be prescribed and given by a vet. Most donkey colic cases, especially mild impactions and gas, respond to medical treatment on the farm. The vet will usually give pain relief and anti-inflammatory medicines, commonly non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as flunixin meglumine or meloxicam, and sometimes antispasmodics such as butylscopolamine to relax the gut, or sedatives such as xylazine or detomidine. Donkeys process several of these drugs differently from horses, so the vet must use donkey-specific knowledge rather than horse doses. For impaction, the vet often passes a stomach tube through the nose to give water, electrolytes (body salts) and a lubricant such as liquid paraffin to soften and move the blockage, sometimes repeated over a day or two. Badly dehydrated donkeys may need fluids into the vein. If hyperlipaemia is found or suspected, the vet will focus on getting energy and nutrition into the donkey quickly, through tempting feeds, tube feeding or glucose-containing fluids, and treat the underlying cause. Worms, dental problems and sand are dealt with once the donkey is stable, for example by the vet planning a suitable dewormer and dental rasping. Antibiotics are not routine for colic and should only be used when the vet finds a specific reason, because unnecessary use encourages antimicrobial resistance. A twisted or strangulated gut needs surgery, which is rarely available or affordable in most parts of Kenya, so in such cases the vet may advise humane euthanasia to end suffering. After treatment, feed is reintroduced slowly in small amounts of soft, moist forage under the vet's guidance. If the donkey's milk is used or the animal may enter the food chain, ask the vet about withdrawal periods for every drug given and follow them.
prevention: Make sure clean water is always available, and give working donkeys time to drink before, during and after work; in cold highland mornings, offering slightly warmed or sun-warmed water can encourage drinking.
Feed plenty of good-quality roughage such as grass or hay little and often through the day, and avoid feeding only straw, stover or very coarse husks, especially to older donkeys.

Make any change in diet gradually over one to two weeks, including when lush grass appears at the start of the long and short rains, and avoid sudden feeding of grain, maize bran, bread or kitchen waste.

Have the teeth checked by a vet or trained equine dental worker at least once a year, and more often for older donkeys; watch for signs such as dropping food, slow chewing, long fibres in droppings or weight loss.
Deworm regularly according to a plan agreed with your vet or County Veterinary Officer, ideally guided by dung egg counts, and pick up droppings from small paddocks and bomas to reduce re-infection.
Feed off the ground using a feeder, sack or clean surface, and avoid grazing on bare, sandy land to reduce sand intake.
Keep donkeys away from rubbish heaps, markets and plastic waste, and remove plastic bags, ropes and twine from feeding areas.
Avoid overworking and overloading donkeys, give rest days, keep donkeys at a healthy body condition rather than fat, and keep them with a companion to reduce stress.
detail.impact: For many Kenyan families, a donkey is a working partner that carries water, firewood, farm produce and goods to market and earns daily income through carting. A donkey with colic cannot work, so the household may lose income, have to buy water or pay for transport while it recovers. Vet fees, medicines and repeat visits add costs, and severe cases can end in the loss of the donkey, which is expensive to replace. Repeated colic often points to underlying problems such as poor teeth, worms or poor water access, which also reduce the donkey's working life and strength. Prevention through water, sensible feeding, deworming and dental care is far cheaper than treatment and keeps the donkey working for many more years.
detail.humanHealth: Colic itself does not infect people. However, a donkey in pain can kick, bite, fall or roll suddenly, so stay out of reach of its legs, never stand directly behind or under it, and keep children away. If the donkey's milk is used or the animal may enter the food chain, any drugs given by the vet will have withdrawal periods; follow the vet's advice so that medicine residues do not reach people. Wash your hands after handling droppings, as donkey dung can carry some germs.
detail.outlook: Many donkeys with mild impaction or gas colic recover well if a vet treats them early and feeding is restarted carefully. The outlook becomes worse the longer colic goes unnoticed, which is a real risk because donkeys hide pain so well. Signs of a poorer outlook include a very fast heart rate, dark or purple gums, no gut sounds, a swollen belly, severe or uncontrolled pain, and fluid coming back up the stomach tube, which may mean a twisted or strangulated gut. Hyperlipaemia greatly reduces the chance of survival, so getting the donkey eating again quickly is vital. Donkeys that recover may get colic again unless the cause, such as bad teeth, worms, poor water access or coarse feed, is corrected.

faqs.q: My donkey is just standing quietly and not eating. Could that really be colic?
faqs.a: Yes. Unlike horses, many donkeys do not roll or kick when they have belly pain. Often the only signs are dullness, standing with the head low, not eating and passing fewer droppings. Any donkey that suddenly stops eating should be treated as an emergency, both because of possible colic and because not eating can trigger hyperlipaemia. Call a vet rather than waiting to see if it gets better.

faqs.q: Can I give my donkey cooking oil, paraffin or a painkiller before the vet comes?
faqs.a: No. Drenching oil or any liquid by mouth can go down the windpipe into the lungs and cause pneumonia or death, and paraffin and many home remedies are harmful. Painkillers, including human tablets like paracetamol, can mask the signs the vet needs to judge how serious the colic is, and some are dangerous at the wrong dose. Remove feed, keep water available, keep the donkey safe and calm, and let the vet decide on treatment.

faqs.q: Should I keep walking my donkey all night so it does not roll?
faqs.a: Usually not. Gentle walking for short periods can help if the donkey is rolling violently and you can do it safely, but long, forced walking exhausts the donkey and you. A quiet donkey that lies down calmly can be allowed to rest in a safe, soft, shaded place. Rolling does not by itself twist the gut; a twist is usually the cause of severe pain, not the result. Your safety matters too, so stay clear of thrashing legs.

faqs.q: How soon can my donkey go back to work after colic?
faqs.a: This depends on the cause and how quickly it recovers, so follow your vet's advice. Most donkeys need at least a few days of rest, with small, frequent meals of soft, moist forage and plenty of water, before slowly returning to light work. Watch closely for normal appetite, regular soft droppings and good energy. Returning to heavy carting too soon, especially in hot weather, can bring the colic back.

faqs.q: Why does my old donkey keep getting colic?
faqs.a: Repeated colic in older donkeys is very often linked to dental problems. Worn, loose, missing or sharp teeth mean food is not chewed properly and forms impactions. Other common reasons are not drinking enough, very coarse feed, worms and eating sand or plastic. Ask a vet to check the teeth and deworming history, and change to softer, chopped or soaked feeds if the teeth are poor.

faqs.q: Can a rehydration or digestive supplement replace the vet?
faqs.a: No. Supplements cannot clear a blockage or fix a twisted gut, and colic always needs a vet. Once the vet has treated the donkey and confirmed it can safely drink and eat, an oral rehydration product added to drinking water may help encourage drinking and replace body salts, and a digestive support product may be used while feed is reintroduced. Always ask your vet first and use them only as support alongside proper treatment and management.

products.role: After the vet has examined and treated the donkey and agrees it can drink normally, RE-COVER mixed in fresh drinking water can help replace water and body salts and encourage drinking during recovery and in hot weather, since dehydration is a major cause of impaction colic. Offer it as a choice alongside plain water, never drench it, and never use it instead of calling the vet.

During recovery, when the vet advises slowly reintroducing feed, K-DIGEST can be used as digestive stress support while the donkey returns to normal eating. It is an aid alongside vet treatment, gradual diet changes, dental care and deworming, not a treatment for colic itself.

card.headline: Long, curled 'slipper' hooves and lameness
card.look: The front of the hooves grows long and may curl up like a slipper, and the donkey walks stiffly or not at all. With laminitis it may rock its weight back onto its heels, shift from foot to foot, lie down more than usual, and the hooves feel hot.
card.action: Stop all work, move the donkey onto soft ground or deep bedding, remove grain and lush grass, keep it eating hay or dry grass, and call your vet today.

detail.summary: Donkey hooves grow all the time. On soft, wet or sandy ground they do not wear down, so they grow long, crack and curl, straining the legs and joints. Laminitis is a painful inflammation of the tissues that hold the hoof wall to the bone inside the foot. It is often linked to rich feed, obesity and hormone problems, and long, neglected hooves make it worse. Both conditions cause serious, often hidden pain, stop a donkey working, and can become permanent or even fatal if ignored.
detail.cause: Inside each hoof, the coffin bone (also called the pedal bone, the last bone of the leg) hangs from the inner hoof wall by thousands of thin, folded layers of tissue called laminae. Think of them like the interlocking fingers of two hands. In laminitis these laminae become inflamed and weak. Blood flow in the foot is disturbed, the tissue swells inside the rigid hoof capsule, and this causes intense pain. If the damage is severe, the bone can tilt downwards (rotation) or drop (sinking) inside the hoof, and in the worst cases press through the sole; this is often called founder. Common triggers in donkeys are too much rich feed (grain, maize bran, dairy meal, kitchen leftovers, lush rain-season grass), obesity, and hormone disorders: insulin problems linked to being fat (sometimes called equine metabolic syndrome) and, in older donkeys, a pituitary gland disorder called PPID or Cushing's disease. Laminitis can also follow a severe infection or toxaemia, such as a retained afterbirth after foaling, colic, or heavy overloading on one leg when the other leg is injured. Overgrown hooves cause problems in a different way. Donkeys evolved on dry, hard, stony ground that wears the hoof naturally. Where the ground is soft, wet or the donkey is kept in a muddy pen, the toe grows long, the heels collapse or grow too high, and the hoof starts to curl. This changes the angle of the leg, strains tendons and joints, lets dirt and germs get into cracks and the white line (the join between wall and sole), and puts extra pulling force on the laminae, so a donkey with neglected feet is more likely to develop or suffer badly from laminitis.
spread: Neither condition is contagious; they do not pass from one donkey to another, but donkeys kept under the same poor management often suffer together.
Lack of regular trimming lets hooves grow long and out of shape, especially when donkeys stand on soft soil, mud, sand or manure where there is little natural wear.
Sudden access to rich feed is a classic trigger, such as a donkey breaking into a grain store, eating maize bran, dairy meal or chicken feed, or being fed leftovers and sweet foods.
Lush, fast-growing grass in the long and short rains, or after a dry spell, is high in sugars and can trigger laminitis in fat or sensitive donkeys.
Obesity and hormone problems (insulin dysregulation and, in older donkeys, PPID) make the feet much more sensitive to laminitis.
Serious illness such as a retained afterbirth, womb infection, severe diarrhoea or colic can release toxins that damage the laminae.
Standing on one leg for a long time because the other leg is injured can cause laminitis in the healthy, overloaded foot.
Constantly wet, dirty standing areas soften the horn, encourage thrush and cracks, and make overgrown feet worse.
detail.atRisk: Any donkey can be affected, but some are at higher risk. Fat donkeys, especially those with a thick, hard crest on the neck and fat pads on the body, are the most likely to get laminitis. Older donkeys (roughly mid-teens and above) are at risk of PPID, which often shows as a long, curly coat that does not shed, and these animals are prone to repeated laminitis. Pet, companion and lightly worked donkeys kept on good grass or fed generously are at higher risk than lean, hard-working ones. Overgrown hooves are most common in donkeys kept in wetter highland areas of Kenya and East Africa, in muddy or manure-filled pens, in zero-grazing or tethered systems with little movement, and wherever no trained hoof trimmer is available. Jennies (female donkeys) that have recently foaled and retained the afterbirth are at risk of laminitis from toxaemia. Risk rises during the long and short rains when grass grows fast and the ground stays soft and wet.

early: The toe of the hoof looks longer than normal, with flaring, chipped or cracked edges, or the hoof shape is uneven between feet.
The donkey is slower than usual, reluctant to walk on hard or stony ground, or takes short, careful steps.
It shifts its weight from one foot to another when standing, or rests a front foot more often than normal.
The hoof wall feels warmer than usual when you hold your hand on it, especially compared with a healthy donkey's feet.
You can feel a stronger, bounding pulse at the back of the fetlock (just above the hoof), called the digital pulse, which is normally hard to feel.
The donkey lies down more than usual, is quiet, or is slower to come for food; donkeys are very stoic and these small changes may be the only sign of pain.
Bad-smelling black material in the grooves beside the frog (the soft V-shaped part of the sole) may show thrush in neglected feet.
advanced: The hooves are very long and curled up at the toe like a slipper or ski, sometimes twisted to one side, so the donkey walks on its heels or the side of the hoof.
The donkey stands rocked back with its front feet pushed forward and its weight on its heels and hind legs, to take weight off the painful toes.
It refuses to move, or moves only with great difficulty, and may lie flat for long periods and be unwilling to get up.
Hooves are clearly hot, with a strong, pounding digital pulse in two or more feet.
Rings or ridges on the hoof wall that are wider at the heel than the toe, a dished front wall, or a dropped, flat or bulging sole show long-standing or past laminitis.
A separated, crumbly white line, a bruised or red-tinged sole, or pus coming from the coronet (the hairline at the top of the hoof) or sole.
Loss of appetite and dullness; in a donkey this is an emergency because not eating can quickly lead to hyperlipaemia, a dangerous build-up of fat in the blood.

lookalikes.name: Hoof abscess
lookalikes.howToTell: An abscess is a pocket of pus inside the hoof. It usually causes sudden, severe lameness in just one leg, sometimes so bad the donkey will not put the foot down. Laminitis more often affects both front feet. An abscess may burst out at the coronet or sole, and the vet can find a very sensitive spot with hoof testers. The two can occur together, so the vet should still check.

lookalikes.name: Thrush and white line disease (seedy toe)
lookalikes.howToTell: These are infections of the horn in dirty, wet or overgrown feet. Thrush shows as black, foul-smelling material in the frog grooves; white line disease shows as crumbly, hollow horn where the wall meets the sole. They cause soreness but usually not the strong heat, bounding pulse and rocked-back stance of laminitis.

lookalikes.name: Arthritis or old joint injury
lookalikes.howToTell: Older and hard-worked donkeys often have stiff joints. The lameness tends to improve as the donkey warms up, the joints may be swollen or thickened, and the hooves are not usually hot with a strong digital pulse. A vet may need to examine and X-ray to tell the difference.

lookalikes.name: Tetanus
lookalikes.howToTell: Tetanus can cause a stiff, 'sawhorse' stance that looks like a laminitic donkey reluctant to move. However, tetanus also causes a stiff neck and tail, ears held rigidly, flared nostrils, jaw stiffness and the third eyelid flicking across the eye when startled. The hooves are not hot. Tetanus is an emergency and needs a vet immediately.

detail.diagnosis: The vet will watch the donkey stand and walk, look closely at the shape and length of every hoof, feel each foot for heat and the digital pulse, and use hoof testers (a large pincer tool) to find painful areas. Cleaning and paring the sole helps show bruising, white line separation or abscesses. Where available, X-rays of the feet show the length of the hoof and whether the coffin bone has rotated or sunk, which guides trimming and tells how serious the case is. The vet may take blood to check for insulin problems or PPID, especially in fat or older donkeys, and to check blood fat levels if the donkey has stopped eating. They will also ask about recent feed and management to find the trigger. To help, tell the vet when you first noticed the problem, what the donkey has been eating (including any grain, bran or access to lush pasture), whether it has been eating and drinking normally, its approximate age, recent foaling or illness, any medicines given, and when the feet were last trimmed. Keep the donkey standing on soft ground nearby so it does not have to walk far for the examination.
firstSteps: Stop all work and riding immediately; a lame or laminitic donkey should not carry loads or pull carts until the vet says it is safe.

Move the donkey a short, slow distance to a small, dry pen or stable with soft footing such as deep sand, wood shavings or clean dry bedding, so the soles are supported and it can lie down comfortably.
Remove all grain, maize bran, dairy meal, kitchen scraps and sweet foods, and keep it off lush grass, but do not starve it; give clean, dry hay or mature dry grass, or barley straw if available.
Make sure it keeps eating and drinking, with clean fresh water always within easy reach; if a donkey stops eating for even a day, tell the vet urgently because of the risk of hyperlipaemia.
Keep a calm companion donkey nearby, as donkeys bond strongly and stress from separation can make them stop eating.
Provide shade and shelter from rain, and keep the standing area clean and dry.

Do not force the donkey to walk, do not attempt heavy trimming of a laminitic foot yourself, and do not give painkillers or other medicines from the agrovet without a vet's advice, as some horse medicines and doses are not right for donkeys.
Write down when signs started, which feet are hot, what it has eaten and any recent illness, and call your vet or County Veterinary Officer the same day.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment aims to control pain, protect the inside of the foot, correct the hoof shape and remove the trigger. Vets commonly use anti-inflammatory painkillers from the NSAID group, such as phenylbutazone, flunixin or meloxicam. Donkeys process several of these drugs differently from horses, so the choice, dose and timing must be decided by a vet who knows donkeys; never use horse instructions or leftover medicine. Strict rest on deep, soft bedding is usually advised, sometimes with frog or sole supports, padding or special boots fitted by the vet or a trained farrier. Overgrown hooves are trimmed back gradually and carefully, often over several sessions, guided by X-rays if available, to bring the toe back and realign the foot without causing more pain or damage. Abscesses are opened and drained, and the foot kept clean and covered. Antibiotics are only needed if there is a deep infection; they do not treat laminitis itself, and using them without need adds to antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to medicines. The vet will plan a diet change, usually a weight-loss plan for fat donkeys based on hay, straw and limited grazing, and may treat PPID with prescribed medication where diagnosed. A donkey that has stopped eating may need urgent fluids and nutrition. Expect recovery from laminitis to take weeks to months, with repeat visits and trims. If a donkey's milk is used or the animal may enter the food chain, follow the withdrawal period the vet gives for each drug before milk or meat is used.
prevention: Have hooves checked and trimmed by a trained farrier or hoof trimmer about every 6 to 10 weeks, more often on soft or wet ground; welfare organisations working with donkeys in Kenya can help locate trained trimmers in some counties.
Pick out and look at your donkey's feet regularly, ideally daily or several times a week, checking for cracks, smell, stones, heat and changes in length.
Keep donkeys lean: feed mainly fibre such as hay, mature dry grass or straw, and avoid or strictly limit grain, maize bran, dairy meal, bread and kitchen scraps.
Control grazing during the long and short rains when grass is lush; use a smaller paddock, a dry yard with hay, or limit grazing time for fat or previously laminitic donkeys.
Learn to body condition score your donkey; feel the neck crest, ribs, back and rump, and ask your vet to show you what a healthy donkey feels like, as donkeys store fat in patches.
Provide a dry, hard standing area such as gravel, murram or concrete, away from mud and manure, so hooves stay strong and some natural wear occurs.
Store grain and concentrates securely so donkeys cannot break in and gorge.
Call the vet early for older donkeys with a long coat that does not shed, drinking or urinating more, or repeated laminitis, as this may be PPID that can be managed.

Make sure retained afterbirths, colic and severe infections get prompt veterinary care, and keep donkeys vaccinated against tetanus as advised by your vet, since foot wounds and abscesses can let tetanus in.
detail.impact: In Kenya and East Africa, many donkeys carry water, firewood, produce and goods to market, and pull carts that earn the household's daily income. A lame donkey cannot work, so the family loses income and must carry loads by hand or hire transport. Long, untreated hooves shorten a donkey's working life by damaging joints and tendons, and laminitis can leave it permanently lame or lead to it being put down on welfare grounds, which is a large loss given the cost of a replacement donkey. Vet visits, X-rays, repeated trimming and months of rest add cost, while prevention through regular trimming and sensible feeding costs far less. Severe lameness and neglected feet are also a welfare concern and can bring problems with welfare inspections where donkeys work at markets and in towns.
detail.humanHealth: Laminitis and overgrown hooves do not infect people. If a donkey is treated with painkillers or antibiotics and its milk is consumed or sold, or it may enter the food chain, drug residues can remain; follow the vet's withdrawal period before using milk or meat. Take care when handling painful feet, as a sore donkey may kick, and keep your own tetanus vaccination up to date if you handle hooves and wounds.
detail.outlook: Overgrown hooves that are caught early usually respond well to a series of careful trims, and most donkeys return to comfortable work. Very long, twisted hooves that have been neglected for years may have caused lasting changes to joints and bones, and some lameness may remain. With laminitis, the outlook depends on how severe it is, how quickly treatment starts and whether the coffin bone has rotated or sunk. Mild cases treated early can recover well over weeks to a few months. Severe cases with major bone movement, sole penetration or repeated attacks have a guarded to poor outlook, and some donkeys must be put to sleep to end their suffering. Donkeys that have had laminitis once are more likely to get it again, so lifelong weight control, careful feeding and regular trimming are essential. A donkey that stops eating because of pain faces the added danger of hyperlipaemia, which can be fatal, so fast action matters.

faqs.q: How often should my donkey's hooves be trimmed?
faqs.a: Most donkeys need a trim about every 6 to 10 weeks, but it depends on the ground and the individual. Donkeys on soft, wet soil or in muddy pens often need trimming more often, while working donkeys on hard, stony ground may wear their feet more. Check the feet often; if the toe is getting long, the hoof is flaring or cracking, or the donkey walks differently, it is time for a trim.

faqs.q: Can I trim my donkey's hooves myself?
faqs.a: Light maintenance is possible after proper training, but trimming the wrong way can lame a donkey. Donkey hooves are shaped differently from horse hooves, with more upright walls and a different angle, so horse-style trimming can damage them. Very overgrown or laminitic feet should always be trimmed by a trained farrier or under a vet's guidance, often over several sessions. Ask your vet or a donkey welfare organisation about training.

faqs.q: Why does my donkey get laminitis when it is fed well?
faqs.a: Donkeys are built to survive on dry, poor-quality grazing. Rich feeds such as grain, maize bran, dairy meal and lush rain-season grass contain more sugar and starch than their bodies can handle. This makes them fat and can upset insulin levels, which damages the laminae in the feet. A healthy donkey diet is mostly fibre such as hay, straw and mature grass, with concentrates only if the vet or nutrition adviser recommends them.

faqs.q: Can I give my donkey painkillers from the agrovet?
faqs.a: Please do not, unless a vet has examined the donkey and prescribed them. Donkeys break down some common painkillers differently from horses, so horse doses and timings can be wrong. Some medicines are dangerous in a dehydrated or sick donkey, and painkillers can hide how bad the problem is, so the donkey may walk and damage its feet further. Your vet will choose a safe drug and dose.

faqs.q: Should I starve my fat donkey to help its laminitis?
faqs.a: No. Donkeys must never be starved or made to lose weight quickly. When a donkey stops eating or is suddenly underfed, its body releases fat into the blood, which can cause hyperlipaemia, a life-threatening condition. Weight loss must be slow, using hay, straw or dry grass and limited grazing, following your vet's plan.

faqs.q: Will a donkey with laminitis ever work again?
faqs.a: Many donkeys with mild laminitis that is treated early return to light or normal work after a period of rest and careful trimming. Donkeys with severe laminitis, where the bone inside the foot has moved a lot, may only manage light duties or a quiet life as a companion. Your vet can judge this from the examination and, if possible, X-rays, and will advise when and how to bring the donkey back into work slowly.

card.headline: Raw sores where the harness rubs
card.look: Patches of hair loss, swelling or raw, weeping skin on the withers, back, girth, chest or under the tail. Flies gather on them, and the donkey flinches or moves away when the harness comes near.
card.action: Stop working the donkey, remove the harness and pad, and keep all pressure off the sore until it has healed and the cause is fixed.

detail.summary: Harness and saddle wounds are pressure and rubbing injuries caused by equipment that does not fit, loads that are too heavy or unbalanced, and long working hours. They start as small bald or swollen patches and can quickly become open, infected sores full of flies and maggots. They are among the most common health problems of working donkeys in Kenya and East Africa. They cause real pain, cost working days, and open the door to tetanus, a deadly disease to which donkeys are very sensitive.
detail.cause: These wounds are caused by pressure and friction on the skin. When a pack saddle, cart pad, breastband, girth, crupper (the strap under the tail) or breeching (the strap around the hindquarters) presses hard on one spot, it squeezes the small blood vessels in the skin shut. Without blood, the skin and tissue underneath starve of oxygen and begin to die. If the equipment also slides back and forth, it rubs the hair off and wears through the skin like sandpaper. Hard or rough materials make this much worse. Examples are nylon rope, wire, plastic sacks, sharp metal parts, knots and unpadded wooden saddles. So do sweat, wet rain-soaked pads, and dried mud or dirt stuck in the harness. Thin donkeys are at special risk because their spine, withers and hip bones stick out with little muscle or fat to cushion them. Once the skin is broken, bacteria from soil, dung and dirty harness enter the wound and cause infection, pus and swelling. Flies are drawn to the smell. Some lay eggs that hatch into maggots (fly larvae that eat flesh), a condition called myiasis. Others carry Habronema worm larvae, which cause 'summer sores': wounds that refuse to heal. Deep or dirty wounds can also let in the tetanus germ (Clostridium tetani), which lives in soil and dung. Tetanus is often fatal in donkeys.
spread: These wounds are not contagious. One donkey cannot catch them from another. But the same poor harness and work habits usually affect every donkey on the farm or in the group.

Badly fitting equipment is the main trigger. Common faults are saddles and pads that are too small, too thin, lumpy or worn. Others are breastbands that sit too high on the windpipe or too low on the shoulder points, and cruppers made of thin rope.

Carts that are unbalanced cause many wounds. If the load sits too far forward, the shafts push down on the back and withers. If it sits too far back, the belly band lifts and rubs. Shafts set at the wrong height for the donkey do the same.
Overloading and long working hours without rest add heavy, constant pressure on the same spots. This is common when carrying water, firewood, building sand or farm produce to market.
Wet, dirty or sweaty harness that is never cleaned or dried rubs harder and carries germs straight into small cuts.
Working a donkey that already has a small sore makes it bigger and deeper every day.

Flies, especially in warm, wet weather during the long and short rains, turn small wounds into infected, maggot-filled sores. They also spread Habronema larvae from wound to wound and from donkey to donkey.
detail.atRisk: Any working donkey can get harness wounds. The highest risk is in donkeys pulling carts or carrying packs every day, such as water vendors, traders, building-sand haulers and farmers taking produce to market. Thin or old donkeys and those with poor body condition are especially at risk, because their bones stand out. So are young donkeys put to work before they are fully grown, and donkeys working on hilly or rough roads. Donkeys on hire or shared between several handlers often suffer most, because nobody owns the duty of checking the harness. Wounds increase in the rainy seasons, when pads stay wet and flies are many. They also increase in the dry, hot months, when donkeys sweat and work longer distances to fetch water. Both peri-urban cart work and pastoral pack work see many cases.

early: A warm, slightly swollen or tender patch where the harness sits, often on the withers, along the spine, behind the elbows (girth area), on the chest or at the base of the tail.
Hair that is rubbed short, broken or missing in the shape of the pad, strap or shaft.
Dry, rough or scaly skin, or a small graze, under the harness.
The donkey flinches, dips its back, lays its ears back or moves away when you touch the area or bring the saddle or harness close.
Patches of white hair growing on the withers or back. This is a sign of old pressure damage and shows the harness has been hurting the donkey for some time.
Uneven sweat marks under the saddle after work, with dry spots where pressure was highest.
advanced: Open, raw, red or pink sores that weep clear fluid, blood or pus.
Thick scabs, crusts or a hard, leathery dead patch of skin (called a 'sitfast') that does not lift off.
Swelling that is hot and painful, sometimes a soft lump full of pus (an abscess).
A bad smell from the wound, and flies clustering on it. Maggots may be seen moving inside.
Wounds that keep growing extra red, lumpy flesh and refuse to heal for weeks, sometimes with small yellow gritty spots. These may be summer sores caused by Habronema.
The donkey is dull, eats less, loses weight or refuses to move forward when harnessed.
Stiffness, difficulty opening the mouth, a stiff tail, a raised third eyelid, or jumpiness at noise. These are signs of tetanus and are an emergency.

lookalikes.name: Sarcoid (a common skin tumour in donkeys)
lookalikes.howToTell: Sarcoids are lumps or flat, wart-like, hairless patches that slowly grow. They often appear around the eyes, ears, groin, chest or legs, not only where the harness rubs. They do not heal with rest and may bleed when rubbed. A harness wound improves once pressure is removed. If a 'wound' keeps growing, ask the vet to check for sarcoid. Never cut or burn it yourself, because handling can make sarcoids worse.

lookalikes.name: Rain scald (dermatophilosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Rain scald happens in wet weather. It shows as many small crusty scabs along the back and rump that lift off with tufts of hair, like the tip of a paintbrush. The skin underneath is pink and moist. It is spread over a wide area rather than in the exact shape of a pad or strap, and it can appear in donkeys that are not working.

lookalikes.name: Mange, lice or ringworm
lookalikes.howToTell: These cause patchy hair loss and crusting that can appear anywhere on the body, including the head, neck and legs. Mange and lice usually cause strong itching, so the donkey rubs on posts and walls. Ringworm forms round, grey, scaly bald patches. Several donkeys are often affected, and the patches do not match where the harness sits.

lookalikes.name: Summer sores (habronemiasis)
lookalikes.howToTell: This is often a complication of a harness wound rather than a separate problem. Suspect it if a wound that should be healing instead grows lumpy, red, bleeding flesh with yellow gritty grains. It is worse in fly seasons and keeps coming back. A vet can confirm it and treat the worm larvae.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or animal health officer usually recognises harness wounds by looking at where they are and matching them to the equipment. They will examine the donkey's whole body and score its body condition. They will gently feel and probe the wound to judge how deep it goes, and check whether it involves muscle, the spine or the withers bones. They will look for pus pockets, dead tissue and maggots, and check for signs of tetanus. A good vet will also ask to see the donkey harnessed or loaded, to find exactly which part is causing the damage. Fixing that is half the treatment. If a wound does not heal as expected, the vet may take a swab to grow and identify the bacteria and choose the right antibiotic. A small tissue sample (biopsy) can rule out sarcoid or summer sores, and an X-ray may be needed if bone infection is suspected. To help the vet, keep the harness, saddle, pads and straps that the donkey was using, and do not wash or change them first. Note when you first saw the sore and how many hours and what loads the donkey has been working. Write down anything you have already put on the wound and whether the donkey has ever had a tetanus vaccine.
firstSteps: Stop work immediately and take off the saddle, pads and harness. Any further use will make the wound deeper and more painful.
Move the donkey to shade with clean drinking water and good forage. A tired, hot working donkey also needs rest and water to recover.

Gently clean the sore with plenty of clean water that has been boiled and cooled. You may add a little salt (about one teaspoon per litre). Pour it over the wound to wash away dirt and loose hair without scrubbing.
Do not put on used engine oil, battery acid, paraffin, cow dung, ash, chilli, strong detergent or hot irons. These common home remedies burn the tissue, delay healing and can poison the donkey.
Protect the wound from flies by keeping the donkey in a shaded, clean area away from dung heaps. Check the wound twice a day for maggots, and tell the vet straight away if you see any.
Wear gloves or wash your hands well with soap after touching the wound, and keep any cuts on your own hands covered.
Write down where the wounds are, how big they are, which harness part touches that spot, and what loads and hours the donkey has worked. Then take a photo if you can.

Call your vet or animal health officer, especially if the wound is deep, smells bad, has maggots, is near the spine or withers, or the donkey has not had a tetanus vaccine. Also call if the donkey becomes stiff or stops eating.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on how deep and dirty the wound is, but rest from the harness is always the most important part. The vet will first clean the wound thoroughly. They may sedate the donkey and numb the area to cut away dead skin, pus and any sitfast, and to remove all maggots. Deep pus pockets may need to be opened and drained. The vet will then advise on daily cleaning and may provide an antiseptic wound dressing or wound spray, often combined with a fly repellent. Because many wounds are contaminated with soil and dung, the vet will think about tetanus protection. This usually means tetanus antitoxin for immediate protection and tetanus toxoid vaccine for longer-term protection, depending on the donkey's vaccination history. For deep, infected or swollen wounds, the vet may prescribe antibiotics such as a penicillin-type drug or another suitable class. Antibiotics are not needed for every shallow rub. Using them only when needed, and finishing the full course as prescribed, helps prevent antimicrobial resistance (germs no longer responding to medicines). The vet may also give pain relief, usually an anti-inflammatory drug. Donkeys break down several common horse drugs at a different speed from horses, so treatment must be prescribed and dosed by a vet who knows donkeys. Never borrow horse or cattle doses. Wounds that may be summer sores are often treated with a dewormer from the avermectin group, such as ivermectin, together with wound care. Some badly damaged withers or chronic wounds may need surgery. Where donkey milk or meat is used, ask the vet about withdrawal periods for every drug given. Expect shallow wounds to need days to a few weeks of rest. Deep or infected wounds can take many weeks. The vet will also advise on fixing or replacing the harness, and organisations working on donkey welfare in Kenya can often help with harness improvement.
prevention: Fit the equipment to the donkey, not the donkey to the equipment. Pack saddles and cart pads should be wide, evenly padded and clear of the spine. There should be a gap you can fit your hand through above the withers and backbone.

Use soft, broad padding such as folded clean cloth, sacking stuffed with dry grass or sisal, foam or old blankets. Replace hard nylon rope, wire and thin straps with wide, soft straps, or cover them with cloth or rubber tubing.

Check the breastband sits across the chest below the windpipe and above the shoulder points. The crupper under the tail should be thick, soft and kept clean, and the girth should be firm but not cutting.

Balance the cart so the load sits over the axle. The shafts should ride level with the donkey's sides, without pressing down on the back or lifting the belly band. Keep tyres pumped and wheels greased so the cart rolls easily.
Do not overload. Match the load to the donkey's size, age, condition and the road, and reduce it on hills, rough tracks and hot days. Ask your vet or animal health officer for a sensible load guide.
Give regular rest breaks with water and shade. Take off the harness whenever the donkey is resting for long periods and at the end of every day.

Clean and dry the harness and pads every day, and never put a wet, muddy or sweat-crusted pad back on. Check the donkey's skin under the harness every day for heat, swelling, hair loss or tenderness, and rest it at the very first sign.
Keep donkeys in good body condition with enough forage, clean water and salt, and deworm them as your vet advises. Thin donkeys get wounds much more easily.
Vaccinate working donkeys against tetanus as your vet recommends, and keep a simple record of the dates.
Reduce flies by removing dung daily, keeping shelters clean and dry, and treating every wound early. Do not work very young, very old, sick or heavily pregnant donkeys.
detail.impact: For many Kenyan households a donkey is a business. It carries water for sale, transports building sand, firewood and produce, and takes children's school fees to market in the form of goods. A donkey with a harness wound must rest, and every day of rest is lost income. Chronic or repeated wounds mean many lost weeks a year. Families then have to pay for vet visits, dressings and medicines, or hire another donkey. Painful donkeys work slowly, become difficult to handle and may kick or refuse to move, which can injure handlers. Infected wounds lead to weight loss and a weaker animal. Tetanus following a wound can kill a donkey within days, wiping out the household's main transport and earning asset. Scarred, wounded donkeys also sell for less. Prevention through good harness and sensible loads costs far less than treating wounds.
detail.humanHealth: Harness wounds themselves do not pass to people, but infected wounds carry bacteria from soil and dung, and some wound germs can infect cuts on human skin. Wear gloves or wash your hands well with soap after cleaning wounds, and cover any cuts on your own hands. The tetanus germ that threatens wounded donkeys also lives in soil and dung and can infect people through deep cuts, so people who work with donkeys and in the soil should keep their own tetanus vaccination up to date. If donkey milk or meat is used, respect the drug withdrawal periods your vet gives so that medicine residues do not reach people.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good for fresh, shallow rubs and sores that are caught early, as long as the donkey is rested and the faulty harness is fixed. These usually heal within days to a few weeks, sometimes leaving white hair or a scar. Deep wounds, infected wounds with pus or maggots, wounds over the withers or spine, and old sitfasts take much longer and may need surgery. Some never return to full strength. Recovery is slower in thin, old or poorly fed donkeys and in the rainy fly season. The biggest risk is tetanus, which is often fatal in donkeys even with treatment, so prevention by vaccination matters. If the donkey goes back to work in the same harness and load, the wound will almost always return, usually worse than before.

faqs.q: Can I keep working my donkey if the sore is small?
faqs.a: No. Even a small sore gets deeper every time the harness presses on it, and a few more days of work can turn a small rub into a wound that takes months to heal. Rest the donkey from that harness until the skin is fully healed and the hair is starting to grow back. Then fix the cause before work starts again. If you truly cannot stop all work, ask your vet whether a lighter task with no pressure on the wound is possible. Never work a donkey with an open wound under the harness.

faqs.q: Is it true that used engine oil or cow dung helps the wound heal?
faqs.a: No. These are common practices, but they harm the donkey. Used engine oil contains chemicals that irritate and poison tissue. Cow dung and ash are full of germs, including the tetanus germ. Battery acid, paraffin and chilli burn the skin. All of them delay healing and can cause serious infection. Clean the wound with boiled and cooled water, keep flies off, and use only dressings or sprays recommended by your vet or agrovet professional.

faqs.q: Why does my donkey get the sore in the same place again and again?
faqs.a: A sore that keeps coming back in the same spot means the cause has not changed. Usually one part of the harness, such as a hard knot, a thin strap, a pad that is too small or a shaft set at the wrong height, presses there every day. Look carefully at where the sore is and which part of the equipment touches it. Then change or pad that part, balance the load and reduce the weight. A vet, animal health officer or donkey welfare organisation can help you check the fit.

faqs.q: Does my donkey need a tetanus injection for a harness wound?
faqs.a: Donkeys are very sensitive to tetanus, and harness wounds are often dirty with soil and dung, where the tetanus germ lives. If your donkey has never been vaccinated, or you do not know, tell your vet about the wound quickly. They may give protection straight away and start a vaccination programme. The best plan is to vaccinate all working donkeys against tetanus on a schedule your vet recommends, before wounds happen.

faqs.q: There are maggots in the wound. What should I do?
faqs.a: Call your vet as soon as possible. Maggots eat living flesh and can make a wound much deeper very quickly, and they cause great pain. Until help arrives, keep the donkey in shade away from flies and wash out the wound with clean boiled and cooled water. Do not pour in paraffin, engine oil, diesel or pesticides meant for crops, because these poison the donkey and damage the tissue. The vet will remove the maggots, clean the wound and advise on fly protection.

faqs.q: How do I know when the donkey is ready to work again?
faqs.a: The wound should be completely closed, dry and covered with healthy skin, with no scab, swelling, heat or pain when you press gently. Hair is usually starting to grow back. Before work starts again, the harness must be fixed or replaced. Start with short, light work and check the skin every day. If you see any heat, swelling or tenderness, stop again straight away. Your vet can tell you when deep wounds are strong enough for pressure.
