harness-wounds.seoDescription: Harness and saddle wounds in donkeys: spot sores on withers, back and chest early, give safe first aid, know vet care, and fit harness to stop them returning.

card.headline: Stiff legs, raised tail, sawhorse stance
card.look: The donkey stands rigid with its legs stretched out like a wooden sawhorse, tail held stiffly out, ears pricked and nostrils flared. When startled, a pale membrane may flick across the eye, and it may struggle to open its mouth or chew.
card.action: Move the donkey gently to a quiet, dark, shaded place with water, keep noise and handling to a minimum, and call a vet immediately, because early treatment gives the best chance.

detail.summary: Tetanus is a severe, often fatal disease caused by a poison (toxin) made by bacteria that live in soil and dung and enter the body through wounds. The toxin acts on the nerves and makes the muscles lock in painful, constant stiffness and spasms. Donkeys and horses are among the animals most sensitive to tetanus, and in donkeys it can kill a valuable working animal within days. It is very hard to treat, but easy and cheap to prevent with vaccination.
detail.cause: Tetanus is caused by Clostridium tetani, a bacterium that survives for years in soil, dust and the dung of animals, especially where horses, donkeys and cattle are kept. It forms tough spores (a resting, seed-like form) that cannot grow in open air. When spores get into a deep or dirty wound where there is little oxygen, such as a nail in the hoof, a castration wound, a harness sore or a foal's navel, they wake up and multiply. As they grow they release a powerful toxin called tetanospasmin. This toxin travels along the nerves to the spinal cord and brain. There it blocks the 'brake' signals that normally tell muscles to relax. Without these brakes, muscles stay contracted all the time and over-react to any sound, light or touch. This is why the donkey becomes stiff, cannot open its jaw, holds its tail out and has spasms. The wound itself may be tiny, hidden or already healed by the time signs appear. Signs usually show between about one and three weeks after the injury, but this can be shorter or much longer. Death usually happens because the breathing muscles go into spasm, the animal cannot eat or drink, or food and saliva go into the lungs and cause pneumonia.
spread: Deep puncture wounds are the classic entry point, especially nails, thorns, wire or sharp sticks that go into the sole of the hoof and are often never noticed.
Castration wounds, particularly when done without clean instruments or without tetanus cover, are a common cause in young male donkeys.
Harness, saddle and cart sores, rope burns and wounds from beatings or sticks can let spores in, especially when dung and dust get into the wound.
Newborn foals can be infected through the wet navel stump if they are born on dirty ground or in a dung-filled shed.
Jennies (female donkeys) can be infected after a difficult foaling, through tears in the birth canal or a retained afterbirth.
Other routes include dental problems, ear or skin injuries, dirty injection sites and bite wounds from dogs or other donkeys.
Tetanus does not spread directly from one donkey to another; each case comes from spores in the environment entering a wound.
detail.atRisk: Any unvaccinated donkey of any age can get tetanus, and most donkeys in Kenya and East Africa have never been vaccinated. Working donkeys that pull carts, carry water, firewood or produce on rough roads are at high risk because they often get hoof punctures, harness sores and other injuries. Young males being castrated, newborn foals and jennies that have just foaled are especially vulnerable. Donkeys kept in yards or sheds with heavy dung build-up, near cattle bomas, or on land with scrap metal, nails and broken wire face more spore contact. Risk rises in the rains when ground is muddy and hooves soften, making punctures easier, and in dry seasons when thorny bush causes many small wounds. Pastoral and peri-urban donkeys that are rarely checked or handled may have wounds that nobody notices.

early: Stiffness when walking, short steps, or reluctance to move or turn, which farmers often mistake for tiredness or sore feet.
The tail head is raised and the tail held slightly out from the body instead of hanging loosely.
Ears held stiffly upright and pointing back, nostrils flared and a worried, fixed facial expression.
The third eyelid (a pale membrane in the inner corner of the eye) flicks across the eye when the head is lifted or the donkey is startled by a noise or a clap.
Difficulty chewing, dropping feed, food balls in the cheeks, or eating very slowly; donkeys are stoic, so a quiet donkey off its feed should always be checked.
Over-reaction to noise, light or touch, with sudden jerky movements or twitching when approached.
advanced: The classic 'sawhorse' stance, with all four legs stiff and stretched out and the neck held straight out.
Locked jaw (lockjaw), where the mouth can hardly be opened, with drooling and inability to eat or drink.
Strong muscle spasms that look like fits, often set off by noise, light or touch, sometimes with sweating.
Hard, board-like muscles over the neck, back, belly and legs.
Falling over and being unable to get up, with the legs held rigid; a donkey that goes down usually has a very poor outlook.
Difficulty breathing, high body temperature from the constant muscle work, constipation and inability to pass urine, followed by death if untreated.

lookalikes.name: Laminitis (founder)
lookalikes.howToTell: A donkey with laminitis also stands strangely, but it rocks its weight back onto the heels to take pressure off painful front feet, and the hooves feel hot with a strong pulse above them. It can open its mouth and eat normally, the third eyelid does not flash, and the tail is not held stiffly out.

lookalikes.name: Rabies
lookalikes.howToTell: Rabies usually causes changes in behaviour, such as aggression, unusual biting, depression, paralysis or a strange bray, rather than the rigid, locked muscles of tetanus. Rabies is a deadly notifiable disease that infects people, so if there is any chance of rabies, do not put your hand in the mouth, keep people away and report it to the County Veterinary Officer at once.

lookalikes.name: Lactation tetany (low blood calcium)
lookalikes.howToTell: This mainly affects jennies nursing a foal or heavily worked animals, and causes trembling, stiffness and sometimes a fast 'thumping' heartbeat. There is usually no wound history, the third eyelid flashing is less typical, and a vet will see quick improvement after calcium treatment.

lookalikes.name: Colic or hyperlipaemia
lookalikes.howToTell: Donkeys with colic or hyperlipaemia (a dangerous fat build-up in the blood seen in stressed, off-feed donkeys) are dull, stop eating and may lie down or roll, but their muscles are not locked rigid and they do not over-react to sound. All of these are emergencies, so call the vet either way.

detail.diagnosis: There is no quick farm or lab test for tetanus, so a vet diagnoses it mainly from the signs and the history. The vet will watch the donkey's stance and movement, check for third eyelid flashing by gently lifting the chin or making a sudden noise, test whether the jaw can be opened, and feel the muscles. They will look carefully for a wound, especially on the soles of the hooves, the castration site, the navel of foals, harness areas and the mouth. Blood tests may be used to rule out other problems such as low calcium or hyperlipaemia. If an animal dies, a post-mortem may be done mainly to rule out other causes, as tetanus leaves few clear changes. To help the vet, note when you first saw stiffness, any recent wounds, castration, foaling or injections, whether the donkey was ever vaccinated against tetanus, and whether it is still drinking and passing dung and urine.
firstSteps: Call a vet straight away and describe the stiffness, raised tail, eye signs and jaw problems, because tetanus gets worse quickly and antitoxin works best early.
Move the donkey calmly to a quiet, dark, shaded and well-bedded shed or corner, away from children, dogs, radios, traffic and other noise that can trigger spasms.
Stop all work immediately; do not try to walk, ride or pull the donkey further than needed, and never beat or force it to move.

Place water and soft, wet feed (such as soaked hay or mash) at a height the donkey can reach without bending its stiff neck, but do not force food or liquid into its mouth, as it may choke or inhale it into the lungs.
Check the hooves and body for wounds, nails or thorns, but leave deep wound cleaning and opening to the vet, and note any wounds you find.
Protect yourself and others: a donkey in spasm can fall or kick suddenly, so approach slowly, keep children away and stand to the side, not behind or in front.
If the donkey goes down, give thick soft bedding and pad the head to prevent injury, and wait for the vet rather than trying to lift it alone.
Do not give any medicines, injections or home remedies without the vet's advice, and write down when signs started and what you have seen.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment of tetanus in donkeys is difficult, slow and costly, and even with good care many animals die, so the vet will give an honest view of the chances before starting. Treatment usually aims at four things. First, the vet gives tetanus antitoxin, which neutralises toxin that is still circulating, though it cannot undo toxin already bound to the nerves. Second, antibiotics such as penicillin or metronidazole are used to kill the bacteria still producing toxin, and the vet will open, clean and flush the wound to let air in. Third, sedatives and muscle relaxants are used to calm the donkey and reduce painful spasms, together with a dark, quiet stable. Fourth, supportive care keeps the animal alive while the nerves recover: fluids and liquid feed may be given by stomach tube or drip if it cannot drink, the donkey may be supported in a sling, and the vet may need to help it pass urine and dung. Vaccination with tetanus toxoid is often started at the same time, because surviving tetanus does not give lasting immunity. Recovery, if it happens, takes weeks, and stiffness may slowly ease over a month or more. All medicines must be prescribed and given by a vet; do not buy antibiotics from an agrovet and treat on your own, because wrong use breeds antibiotic resistance and does not neutralise the toxin. If donkey milk or meat is ever used for food, the drug withdrawal periods the vet gives must be followed. Antitoxin is made from horse serum and can rarely cause reactions, which the vet will watch for.
prevention: Vaccinate every donkey against tetanus with tetanus toxoid: a primary course followed by regular boosters on the schedule your vet advises; equine tetanus vaccines are commonly used in donkeys.
Vaccinate pregnant jennies in late pregnancy as your vet advises, so that their first milk (colostrum) gives the newborn foal protection, and plan foal vaccination with the vet.
When an unvaccinated donkey gets a deep wound, ask the vet promptly about tetanus antitoxin and starting vaccination, rather than waiting to see if signs appear.
Have castration done only by a vet or trained animal health worker using clean instruments, with tetanus protection given beforehand.
Keep foaling areas clean and dry, and dip the newborn foal's navel in a suitable disinfectant soon after birth.
Check hooves daily, especially in the rains, remove stones and thorns, and have the hooves trimmed regularly so cracks and punctures are found early.
Fit harnesses, saddles and cart shafts well, pad them, and check for sores every day; rest donkeys with sores until they heal.
Clear yards, sheds and paths of nails, wire, broken glass and scrap metal, and remove dung build-up regularly to reduce spore numbers.
detail.impact: In Kenya, donkeys are working animals that carry water, firewood, farm produce and goods to market, and many families, especially women, depend on them for daily income and to reduce heavy workloads. Losing a donkey to tetanus means lost transport income, more hours spent fetching water by hand, and the cost of buying a replacement. Treatment, when attempted, needs repeated vet visits, medicines and weeks of nursing, and the donkey cannot work during that time. Because the disease is often fatal even with treatment, the money spent may not save the animal. A cheap vaccine given in advance is far less costly than one case of tetanus, which makes vaccination one of the best investments a donkey owner can make.
detail.humanHealth: People cannot catch tetanus from a sick donkey, but they can get tetanus in the same way donkeys do, from soil, dust and dung entering cuts, thorn pricks and nail wounds. Farmers, carters and children who work around donkeys and manure are at risk. Make sure everyone in the household is up to date with tetanus vaccination at the local health facility, wear shoes and gloves when cleaning sheds and handling wounds, and clean any cut promptly and seek medical advice for deep or dirty wounds. A donkey in tetanus spasm can also kick or fall suddenly, so handle it carefully to avoid injury.
detail.outlook: The outlook for a donkey with tetanus is guarded to poor. Donkeys that are treated early, while they can still stand, drink and swallow, and whose signs develop slowly, have the best chance. Animals that go down, cannot drink, have severe spasms or develop signs very quickly after an injury usually die despite treatment. Survivors often begin to improve after the first week or two, and may need several weeks or more to recover fully, but many go back to normal work. Recovery does not protect the donkey in future, so it must be vaccinated afterwards.

faqs.q: Can my other donkeys catch tetanus from the sick one?
faqs.a: No. Tetanus does not pass from animal to animal. Each case comes from spores in soil or dung entering a wound. However, if one donkey got tetanus, the others share the same environment and risks, so this is a good time to vaccinate all of them and check them for wounds.

faqs.q: The wound healed long ago. Can it still be tetanus?
faqs.a: Yes. Signs usually appear one to three weeks after the injury, and sometimes later, so the wound may have healed or been too small to notice, such as a nail prick in the hoof. Tell the vet about any wounds, castration or foaling in the past weeks, even if they look healed.

faqs.q: Will antibiotics from the agrovet cure tetanus?
faqs.a: No, not on their own. Antibiotics can kill the bacteria, but the damage comes from the toxin already attached to the nerves. A vet needs to give antitoxin, clean the wound, control spasms and give supportive care. Using antibiotics without a vet wastes money, delays proper treatment and adds to antibiotic resistance.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for donkeys, and is it expensive?
faqs.a: Yes. Tetanus toxoid vaccines, often the ones made for horses, are used in donkeys and are usually affordable compared to the cost of losing an animal. A donkey needs a first course and then regular boosters. Ask your vet, County Veterinary Officer or a donkey welfare organisation about vaccination; some run vaccination days in donkey-working areas.

faqs.q: If my donkey survives tetanus, is it protected for life?
faqs.a: No. The amount of toxin that causes disease is too small to build lasting immunity, so a donkey that recovers can get tetanus again. It needs to be vaccinated once it is well enough, as your vet advises.

faqs.q: My donkey is stiff but still eating. Should I wait and see?
faqs.a: No. If you see stiffness together with a raised tail, pricked ears, flashing third eyelid or slow chewing, call the vet now. Tetanus usually gets worse over a few days, and treatment works best before the donkey stops drinking or goes down. Laminitis and other problems can also look like stiffness, and they also need a vet.

tetanus.imagePrompt: A grey working donkey standing rigidly in a sawhorse stance with all four legs stiffly stretched out, neck held straight, ears pricked and tail held stiffly away from the body, in a dusty rural Kenyan homestead compound with an acacia tree in the background.
tetanus.seoDescription: Tetanus in donkeys: spot stiff sawhorse stance, raised tail and locked jaw early, what to do before the vet comes, and how vaccination prevents it.

card.headline: Pot belly, rough coat, ribs showing
card.look: The donkey is thin along the back and ribs but has a rounded, dropped belly. Its coat is dull, rough and slow to shed, and it may be weak, cough or show mild colic.
card.action: Weigh or tape the donkey, collect a fresh dung sample, and ask your vet or County Veterinary Officer for a worm egg count and the right dewormer before you treat.

detail.summary: Internal worms are parasites that live inside the donkey's gut, lungs or stomach and feed off the animal. In Kenya almost every donkey that grazes carries some worms. Heavy burdens cause weight loss, weakness, a rough coat, colic and coughing. Because donkeys are tough and hide illness, worms often go unnoticed until the animal is thin and can no longer work well.
detail.cause: Several kinds of parasites are involved. The most important are strongyles, often called red worms. Small strongyles are the most common. Their young stages (larvae) burrow into the wall of the large intestine and can stay hidden there, or 'encysted', for months. When many come out at once, often in late winter-like cool spells or after deworming, they can cause sudden diarrhoea and fast weight loss. Large strongyles are fewer today but their larvae travel through the blood vessels of the gut, damaging them and causing colic (belly pain). Lungworm (Dictyocaulus arnfieldi) lives in the airways. Donkeys are its natural host and often carry it with few signs, but it can cause a long-lasting cough, and it can pass to horses, which suffer more. Bots are not true worms but the larvae (maggots) of the bot fly. The fly lays small yellow eggs on the hair of the legs, chest and shoulders. The donkey licks them, the larvae hatch in the mouth and then attach to the stomach lining for many months. Other parasites include roundworms (Parascaris) in young foals, which can block the gut, tapeworms linked to some types of colic, pinworms that cause tail rubbing, and liver fluke in wet, swampy grazing. Together these parasites steal nutrients, damage the gut lining, cause blood and protein loss, and reduce how well the donkey uses its feed.
spread: Worm eggs pass out in the dung of infected donkeys, horses and mules and hatch into larvae on the grass.
In warm, wet weather, especially during the long and short rains, larvae survive well and climb up wet grass where donkeys eat them.
Communal grazing, shared watering points and overstocked paddocks keep re-infecting donkeys because dung builds up on the ground.
Bot flies lay sticky yellow eggs on the donkey's hair in the warm months, and the donkey swallows the larvae when it licks or scratches itself.
Lungworm larvae are swallowed from contaminated pasture, then travel to the lungs; donkeys grazing with horses can pass lungworm on to them.
Tapeworms are picked up when donkeys eat tiny pasture mites carrying the tapeworm's young stage.
Liver fluke spreads through water snails, so donkeys grazing near swamps, dams and irrigation channels are more exposed.
detail.atRisk: Young donkeys from foals to about two years old carry the heaviest burdens because they have not yet built up resistance. Very old donkeys, pregnant and nursing jennies, and working donkeys that are overworked and underfed also suffer more. Donkeys on communal grazing, roadside verges and small, overused paddocks are at higher risk than those on rotated or rested land. Worm pressure is usually highest during and after the long and short rains, when grass is wet and larvae survive well. Fluke is a problem in wetter highland and lakeside areas. In hot, dry pastoral and ASAL areas fewer larvae survive on pasture, but donkeys there are often already thin from poor feed, so even a moderate worm burden hurts them. Donkeys that have not been dewormed for a long time, or that are dewormed with the wrong product or too little drug, are also at risk.

early: Slow, steady weight loss, with the spine, hip bones and ribs becoming easier to see and feel.
A dull, rough, dry coat that does not shed properly, even when the donkey is eating.
Less energy for work; the donkey tires quickly when pulling a cart or carrying water.
Small yellow bot eggs stuck to the hair of the front legs, chest, shoulders or mane.
Rubbing the tail against walls or posts, leaving a broken, bare-looking tail head (often pinworms).
An occasional dry cough, especially when moving or working.
advanced: A pot belly that hangs down while the back and hindquarters are thin.
Pale gums and inner eyelids, showing anaemia (thin blood from blood loss).
Soft dung or diarrhoea, sometimes sudden and severe, with rapid weight loss.
Swelling under the belly, chest or lower legs from protein loss.
Colic signs: dullness, not eating, lying down more than usual, rolling, looking at or kicking at the belly; in donkeys these signs are often quiet and easy to miss.
A persistent cough, faster breathing or poor recovery after work.
In young foals, poor growth, a big belly and sometimes sudden colic from a blockage of roundworms.

lookalikes.name: Dental problems
lookalikes.howToTell: A donkey with bad teeth also loses weight, but it drops chewed feed balls from its mouth (quidding), chews slowly or on one side, has a bad smell from the mouth, or has whole grain or long fibre in its dung. A vet can check the teeth; many thin donkeys have both teeth and worm problems.

lookalikes.name: Poor feeding and overwork
lookalikes.howToTell: Underfed or overworked donkeys are thin and weak, but they usually improve quickly with more feed and rest. If the donkey stays thin on good feed, has a pot belly, pale gums or a high worm egg count, worms are more likely.

lookalikes.name: Trypanosomiasis (tsetse disease, nagana)
lookalikes.howToTell: In tsetse areas, trypanosomiasis causes weight loss and anaemia like worms, but it often comes with fever, swollen glands, watery eyes and swelling under the belly or legs, and may affect several animals after grazing near bush. A blood test by the vet tells them apart.

lookalikes.name: Respiratory infections such as strangles or dust cough
lookalikes.howToTell: Strangles brings fever, thick yellow discharge from the nose and swollen glands under the jaw. Dust-related cough improves when the donkey is moved to cleaner bedding or feed. Lungworm cough is usually long-lasting, without fever or heavy nasal discharge, and the donkey may otherwise look well.

detail.diagnosis: The vet will look at the donkey's body condition, gums, coat, belly shape, breathing and teeth, and ask about deworming history and grazing. The main test is a faecal egg count, where a fresh dung sample is checked under a microscope to count worm eggs and see which types are present. A special test (Baermann test) looks for lungworm larvae in the dung. Egg counts do not show encysted small strongyle larvae or bots, so the vet also uses the signs and history. A blood test may be done to check for anaemia and low protein, or to rule out trypanosomiasis. If a donkey dies, a post-mortem can show the worms, bots and gut damage directly. Before the vet comes, collect a few balls of fresh dung straight after the donkey passes it, put it in a clean, sealed plastic bag with the air pressed out, label it with the donkey's name and date, and keep it cool and out of the sun. Write down when the donkey was last dewormed, which product was used, and how much it weighs by donkey weigh tape if you have one.
firstSteps: Check the donkey's condition by feeling its ribs, spine and hips, and look at its gums for paleness; write down what you find.
Collect a fresh dung sample in a clean sealed bag, keep it cool, and take it to your vet or ask the County Veterinary Officer where it can be tested.
Reduce the donkey's workload and let it rest until it has been checked, because a weak, wormy donkey can collapse under heavy loads.
Give clean water at all times and good quality hay or grass, and offer feed in small, regular amounts rather than large meals.
If you see colic signs, such as rolling, lying down a lot, not eating or not passing dung, call the vet urgently, because colic can kill donkeys quickly.
Scrape or pick off yellow bot eggs from the legs and shoulders using a bot knife or blunt blade, and burn or bury them.
Pick up dung from the paddock or boma regularly so fewer eggs reach the grass.
Do not give any dewormer until the vet has advised which product suits the worms present and the donkey's weight, age and condition.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment uses dewormers (anthelmintics) chosen by the vet for the worms found. Common groups include macrocyclic lactones such as ivermectin and moxidectin, which act on strongyles, lungworm and bots; benzimidazoles such as fenbendazole, sometimes given as a longer course for encysted small strongyle larvae; pyrantel; and praziquantel for tapeworms. Not every product is safe for every donkey; some are not suitable for very young foals or very thin animals, and the vet will choose accordingly. The most common mistake is underdosing. Donkeys are usually heavier than they look and many farmers guess, so the vet will estimate weight with a donkey weigh tape or chart, not a cattle or horse tape. Underdosing fails to kill worms and helps them become resistant. Resistance to dewormers, especially in small strongyles, is a growing problem worldwide, so the vet may suggest a follow-up egg count about two weeks after treatment to check the drug worked. In a very heavily infected donkey, killing many worms at once can sometimes trigger colic or diarrhoea, so the vet may treat in stages and ask you to watch closely for a few days. Severe cases with diarrhoea, swelling or colic may need fluids, pain relief and supportive care. If donkey milk or meat enters the food chain, the vet will tell you the withdrawal period for the product, the time you must wait after treatment before milk or meat can be used.
prevention: Work with your vet on a deworming plan based on regular faecal egg counts rather than deworming every donkey on a fixed calendar; this saves money and slows drug resistance.
Weigh donkeys with a donkey weigh tape or chart before every treatment so the full dose prescribed by the vet is given.
Use the product the vet recommends for the season and worm type, for example covering bots after the fly season and tapeworms where they are a problem.
Pick up dung from small paddocks and bomas at least a few times a week, and do not spread fresh donkey or horse dung on grazing land.
Rotate grazing where possible, rest paddocks, or graze cattle, sheep or goats behind donkeys, since most donkey worms do not survive in ruminants.
Avoid overstocking, and keep donkeys away from swampy areas and stagnant water where liver fluke snails live.
Remove bot eggs from the coat regularly during the fly season.
Keep new donkeys separate for a period and have them checked and treated by the vet before they join the herd.
Keep donkeys and horses on separate grazing, or treat donkeys for lungworm, to protect horses from lungworm.
Feed well, provide clean water, check teeth yearly and avoid overwork so donkeys can cope with the worms they carry.
detail.impact: For many Kenyan households the donkey is a working partner, carrying water, firewood and produce to market or pulling a cart that earns daily income. A wormy donkey tires quickly, carries less, and needs more rest, which directly cuts what the family can earn or move. Feed is wasted because worms take a share of it, and thin donkeys need longer to recover after the dry season. Young donkeys grow slowly and may never reach full working size. Colic from worms can mean expensive vet visits or the sudden loss of an animal that costs a lot to replace. Repeated use of the wrong dewormer wastes money and helps resistant worms build up on the farm and in communal grazing.
detail.humanHealth: Most donkey worms do not infect people. Very rarely, bot fly larvae can enter human skin or eyes, so wash your hands after picking off bot eggs or handling the coat, and keep hands away from your eyes. Donkeys can carry hydatid cysts, which dogs pick up by eating raw offal, so do not feed raw donkey organs to dogs. If donkey milk or meat is used for food, always respect the withdrawal period given by the vet for any dewormer.
detail.outlook: Most donkeys recover well once the right dewormer is given at the correct weight and their feeding, rest and teeth are put right. Coat and energy often improve within weeks, but regaining lost weight can take months, especially in old or very thin animals. The outlook is poorer when there is severe diarrhoea from encysted small strongyles, heavy swelling from protein loss, or colic from gut damage, and some of these donkeys may not survive even with treatment. Long-term success depends on preventing re-infection through good pasture hygiene, sensible deworming based on egg counts, and using drugs that still work on your farm.

faqs.q: How often should I deworm my donkey?
faqs.a: There is no single right answer for every farm. Many vets now advise testing dung with a faecal egg count and treating the donkeys that carry the most eggs, rather than dosing all animals on a fixed schedule. Young donkeys usually need more attention than adults. Ask your vet to set a plan around your local seasons, such as checking before and after the rains, and to include bot and tapeworm treatment where needed.

faqs.q: Can I use my cattle or goat dewormer on my donkey?
faqs.a: Do not do this without vet advice. Some cattle and goat products are not made or tested for donkeys, can be the wrong strength, or can cause reactions, especially injectable forms. Some worms in donkeys, like bots and tapeworms, are not covered by many ruminant products. Ask your vet or agrovet for a product labelled for horses and donkeys, and dose by weight as the vet directs.

faqs.q: I dewormed my donkey but it is still thin. Why?
faqs.a: There are several possible reasons. The dose may have been too small because the weight was guessed. The worms on your farm may be resistant to that drug. Encysted small strongyle larvae may not have been reached. The donkey may have bad teeth, too little feed, too much work, or another disease such as trypanosomiasis. A vet can do a follow-up egg count, check the teeth and look for other causes.

faqs.q: Can my donkeys give worms to my horses or cattle?
faqs.a: Donkeys share most of their worms with horses and mules, and donkey lungworm is a particular risk to horses because it can give them a bad cough. Most donkey worms do not survive in cattle, sheep or goats, which is why mixed or rotated grazing with ruminants can help clean pastures. Liver fluke is an exception, as it can affect all these animals.

faqs.q: Is it safe to deworm a pregnant jenny or a young foal?
faqs.a: Often yes, but only with products the vet confirms are safe for pregnancy or for that age. Some dewormers are not recommended for very young foals or very thin animals. Controlling worms in the jenny before and after foaling helps protect the foal, which picks up worms from the ground and from its mother's dung. Always tell the vet if the jenny is pregnant or nursing.

faqs.q: What are the yellow dots stuck on my donkey's legs?
faqs.a: These are almost certainly bot fly eggs. The fly glues them to the hair, and when the donkey licks the area the larvae hatch and move to its stomach. Scrape them off with a bot knife or blunt blade and destroy them, and ask your vet about a dewormer that kills bots at the right time of year.

products.role: Vitamin A, D3 and E support for thin, run-down donkeys recovering from a heavy worm burden, especially in the dry season when green feed is scarce, used alongside vet-prescribed deworming, better feeding and rest.

Digestive and liver support during recovery after deworming, helping a donkey whose gut has been stressed by parasites, as an aid to vet treatment and good feeding, not a dewormer or replacement for one.

card.headline: Thin, weak donkey with swollen legs
card.look: The donkey loses weight even when feeding, tires quickly, and has pale gums and puffy swelling on the lower legs, belly or sheath. It may have a fever that comes and goes, and watery eyes.
card.action: Keep the donkey resting in shade with water and call your vet or animal health officer for a blood test before giving any trypanocide drug.

aka: Ndorobo (local name in parts of Kenya)
detail.summary: Trypanosomiasis is a blood disease caused by tiny parasites called trypanosomes. They are spread mainly by tsetse flies (mbung'o) and also by other biting flies such as horse flies and stable flies. In donkeys it is usually a slow, wasting disease: the animal becomes thin, weak and anaemic and can no longer work. Without proper treatment many donkeys slowly decline and can die, and the disease is a major cause of lost working power in tsetse areas of Kenya and East Africa.
detail.cause: The disease is caused by single-celled parasites of the genus Trypanosoma that live and multiply in the blood and body fluids. In donkeys in East Africa the main species are Trypanosoma congolense, Trypanosoma vivax and Trypanosoma brucei brucei, which come mostly from tsetse flies, and Trypanosoma evansi, which causes surra and is carried mechanically by biting flies, especially in camel-keeping areas. When an infected fly bites, trypanosomes enter the blood and multiply in waves. Each wave brings a spell of fever; the body's defences kill many parasites, but the parasites change their outer coat and a new wave appears. Over weeks and months the parasites and the body's reaction destroy red blood cells, causing anaemia (too few red blood cells, which shows as pale gums and weakness). Damage to small blood vessels lets fluid leak into the tissues, which is why the legs, belly, chest and sheath or udder swell. The animal burns energy fighting the infection, so it loses muscle and condition. Some species, especially T. brucei and T. evansi, can also enter the brain and nervous system in later stages, causing wobbliness and abnormal behaviour. The weakened immune system also makes the donkey more likely to pick up other infections.
spread: Tsetse flies (mbung'o) are the main carriers of T. congolense, T. vivax and T. brucei; the parasite develops inside the fly and is passed on when the fly bites a donkey.

Biting flies such as horse flies (tabanids) and stable flies can carry blood with trypanosomes on their mouthparts from a sick animal to a healthy one within minutes, which spreads T. evansi and T. vivax even outside tsetse areas.
Grazing, watering or working donkeys near bush, riverine forest, lake shores and thickets where tsetse rest raises the risk, especially in the morning and late afternoon when flies are active.
Sharing the same needle or syringe between animals during injections or vaccination can pass infected blood directly from one animal to another.
Herding donkeys together with infected cattle, camels, goats or wildlife provides a constant source of parasites for flies to pick up.
Moving donkeys into or through tsetse belts, for example during dry-season migration, trading or transport work, can bring them into contact with infected flies.
Stress from heavy work, long journeys, poor feeding and worms does not cause the disease, but it can make a carrier donkey become clearly sick.
detail.atRisk: Any donkey living in or passing through tsetse areas is at risk, including parts of the Coast, the Lake Victoria basin, the Maasai Mara and other bushy lowland and riverine areas. Donkeys kept with camels in northern and eastern pastoral areas such as Turkana, Marsabit, Isiolo and Wajir are at risk of surra (T. evansi). Working donkeys that are overworked, underfed, heavily wormed or old are more likely to become severely ill. Pregnant jennies may abort, and foals and young donkeys can decline quickly. Risk often rises during and after the rains, when flies are more numerous, and during dry-season movements when herds go to bushy grazing and water points near tsetse habitat. Donkeys are sometimes thought to be more tolerant than horses, but they still suffer, and because donkeys hide illness well, the disease is often noticed late.

early: Fever that comes and goes; the donkey may feel hot, breathe faster or seem dull for a day or two, then appear normal again.
Tiring easily during work, lagging behind, or refusing to pull or carry loads it managed before.
Slight weight loss, with ribs and hip bones becoming easier to see, even though the donkey is still eating.
Watery eyes and a clear discharge from the eyes in some animals.
Paler than normal gums and inner eyelids, which should normally be pink.
A dull coat and slightly reduced interest in food.
advanced: Marked wasting, with a sharp backbone, sunken flanks and thin neck and hindquarters, despite eating.
Very pale or white gums and eyelids from severe anaemia, sometimes with a fast heartbeat you can feel on the left side of the chest.
Soft, puffy swelling (oedema) of the lower legs, under the belly, under the chest, and of the sheath or udder; pressing with a finger may leave a dent.
Severe weakness, stumbling, unwillingness to stand for long, or lying down much more than normal.
Swollen lymph nodes (glands) that can be felt under the skin, for example in front of the shoulder.
Abortion in pregnant jennies and weak or stunted foals.
In some cases wobbly walking, circling, dullness or other nervous signs when the parasites reach the brain.
Collapse and death after weeks to months if not treated.

lookalikes.name: Heavy worm burden (strongyles and other worms)
lookalikes.howToTell: Worms also cause weight loss, pale gums and sometimes belly swelling, but there is usually no fever. A dung sample showing many worm eggs and improvement after vet-advised deworming point to worms. The two problems often occur together, so a blood test is still useful in tsetse areas.

lookalikes.name: Malnutrition and dental problems
lookalikes.howToTell: Donkeys with sharp or missing teeth drop food, chew slowly and have whole grains or long fibres in dung. Starvation loses weight without fever or leg swelling. The donkey usually improves with better feed and dental care, while a donkey with trypanosomiasis keeps wasting despite good feed.

lookalikes.name: Equine piroplasmosis (babesiosis, tick fever)
lookalikes.howToTell: This tick-borne blood parasite disease also causes fever and anaemia, but often shows yellow gums (jaundice) and sometimes dark red or brown urine. Ticks are usually found on the animal. A vet can tell the two apart on a stained blood smear.

lookalikes.name: Dourine
lookalikes.howToTell: Dourine is a related trypanosome disease spread by mating, not flies. It causes swelling of the genitals, raised round skin plaques and later nerve weakness, mostly in breeding animals. Mating history and laboratory tests are needed to separate it, and any suspicion should be discussed with the County Veterinary Officer.

detail.diagnosis: A vet suspects trypanosomiasis from the signs, the area, and the history of tsetse or biting flies. Confirmation needs a blood test. The vet or laboratory examines a drop of fresh blood under the microscope to see moving parasites, and prepares thin and thick stained blood smears to identify the species. Spinning blood in a fine tube (the haematocrit or buffy coat method) measures the packed cell volume, which shows how anaemic the donkey is, and concentrates parasites so they are easier to find. Parasites appear in the blood in waves, so a single negative test does not rule the disease out; samples taken during a fever are more likely to be positive, and repeat tests may be needed. Some laboratories, such as county and KALRO laboratories, can run PCR (a DNA test) or antibody tests, which are more sensitive, especially for T. evansi. At post-mortem a vet may find a thin carcass, watery fluid in tissues and body cavities, pale organs, an enlarged spleen and swollen lymph nodes. To help the vet, record the donkey's temperature morning and evening if you have a thermometer, note when weight loss and swelling started, where the donkey has grazed, worked or travelled, whether tsetse or many biting flies were seen, any drugs already given, and whether other donkeys, cattle or camels in the herd are also sick.
firstSteps: Stop all work immediately and let the donkey rest; working a weak, anaemic donkey can make it collapse.
Move the donkey to a shaded, airy place protected from flies, and keep it away from bushy grazing and water points where tsetse are found.
Provide clean drinking water at all times and good-quality soft hay or grass so the donkey keeps eating; do not force feed.
Check the gums, eyelids and legs, take the temperature if you can, and write down what you see with dates so the vet can follow the pattern.
Look at the rest of the herd, including cattle and camels, for similar thinness, swelling or fever, and keep sick animals apart where possible.
Use a new or properly sterilised needle for every animal if any injections are being given on the farm, to avoid spreading infected blood.
Do not buy and inject a trypanocide from the agrovet without a vet's advice; some of these drugs are dangerous for donkeys at the wrong dose, and wrong use builds drug resistance.
Call your vet, animal health officer or County Veterinary Officer early, because treatment works best before the donkey becomes severely wasted.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be prescribed and given by a vet or under a vet's direct guidance. Vets use drugs called trypanocides, which kill trypanosomes in the blood. Commonly used active ingredients include diminazene aceturate and isometamidium chloride for tsetse-borne trypanosomes, and quinapyramine or melarsomine for T. evansi (surra). The choice depends on which parasite is found, the area and known drug resistance. Donkeys and horses are more sensitive than cattle to some of these drugs, which can cause serious side effects, painful swelling at the injection site or poisoning if given wrongly, so correct product, dose and injection method matter greatly. Drug resistance to trypanocides is a growing problem in East Africa, often linked to underdosing and repeated self-treatment, so the vet may advise a different drug if the donkey does not improve. The vet may also treat worms, advise on feeding to rebuild condition, and recommend rest for several weeks. In some cases a preventive (prophylactic) drug is advised for donkeys that must keep working in tsetse areas. Antibiotics do not kill trypanosomes; they are only used if the vet finds a separate bacterial infection, and they should be used responsibly to avoid antimicrobial resistance. Expect the fever to settle within days after the right treatment, but weight and strength return slowly over weeks. Relapses can occur, so follow-up blood tests may be needed. If donkey milk or meat is used, observe the withdrawal period stated by the vet and on the drug label before any milk or meat is consumed or sold.
prevention: Reduce contact with tsetse by avoiding grazing, watering and resting donkeys in bush, thickets, riverine forest and lake shores where tsetse live, especially in the early morning and late afternoon.

Support community tsetse control, such as blue and black cloth traps and insecticide-treated targets, often run with county veterinary teams and KENTTEC (the Kenya Tsetse and Trypanosomosis Eradication Council).

Protect donkeys with fly repellents or insecticide sprays and pour-ons that are approved for equines, following label and vet advice, and consider insecticide-treated nets around stables in high-risk areas.
Control biting flies around the homestead by removing manure and wet bedding regularly and draining stagnant water, which reduces stable flies and horse flies.
Always use a clean needle for each animal during injections and vaccination, by vets, agrovet staff and farmers alike.
Ask your vet about preventive trypanocide treatment for donkeys that must work or travel in tsetse areas, and never give these drugs without veterinary guidance.
Keep donkeys strong with good feed, clean water, salt, regular deworming, hoof and dental care and fair workloads, so they cope better if infected.
Quarantine new donkeys for a few weeks and ask for a blood test if they come from a tsetse or surra area, and test donkeys after long journeys through such areas.
detail.impact: For many Kenyan families a donkey carries water, firewood, farm produce and goods to market, and earns cash through transport work. A donkey with trypanosomiasis works less, then not at all, so households lose income and family members, often women and children, must carry loads themselves. Treatment, repeated blood tests and lost working days add cost, and wrong or repeated self-treatment wastes money and builds drug resistance. Jennies may abort or raise weak foals, slowing herd growth. Deaths of working donkeys are a heavy loss, as replacing a donkey is expensive. Because the same flies and parasites affect cattle, goats and camels, a sick donkey is also a warning that the whole herd may be at risk.
detail.humanHealth: The trypanosome species that usually cause disease in donkeys (T. congolense, T. vivax and T. brucei brucei) do not infect people. However, in some tsetse areas near the Lake Victoria basin, the related parasite Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense causes human sleeping sickness, and livestock can carry it, so people in these areas should protect themselves from tsetse bites with long sleeves and repellents and see a health worker if they get fever, headache and swollen glands after being bitten. Very rare human infections with T. evansi have been reported elsewhere in the world. Trypanocide drugs can leave residues in milk and meat, so the withdrawal period given by the vet must be respected before any donkey milk or meat is consumed.
detail.outlook: Donkeys treated early, with the right drug for the parasite and a correct dose, often recover well, although regaining weight and full working strength can take weeks to months. The outlook is poorer when the donkey is already severely wasted or very anaemic, is old, pregnant or carrying heavy worms, when nervous signs have appeared, or when the parasites are resistant to the drug used. Relapses and reinfection are common if the donkey goes back to the same fly-infested grazing without protection. Good rest, feeding and fly control after treatment improve the chances of a lasting recovery.

faqs.q: Can I just buy a trypanocide from the agrovet and inject my donkey myself?
faqs.a: It is not advised. Some trypanocides that are commonly used in cattle can be toxic to donkeys if the dose or injection method is wrong, and they can cause severe painful swellings. Self-treatment without a blood test also means you may be treating the wrong disease, such as worms or tick fever. Repeated wrong doses are a major reason trypanocides are failing in Kenya. Ask a vet to confirm the disease and choose and give the right drug.

faqs.q: My donkey tested negative but is still getting thinner. Could it still be trypanosomiasis?
faqs.a: Yes, it is possible. Trypanosomes appear in the blood in waves, and between waves there may be too few to see under a microscope. Ask the vet whether a repeat test during a fever, a buffy coat test, or a PCR or antibody test is available. At the same time the vet should check for other causes such as worms, teeth problems and poor feeding.

faqs.q: We have no tsetse flies in our area. Can donkeys still get this disease?
faqs.a: They can. Trypanosoma evansi, which causes surra, and Trypanosoma vivax can be spread by ordinary biting flies such as horse flies and stable flies, and by shared needles. This is why donkeys kept with camels in northern Kenya can get surra far from tsetse areas. Donkeys can also pick up infection while travelling through tsetse areas and become sick after returning home.

faqs.q: Will my donkey be immune after it recovers?
faqs.a: No. Donkeys do not develop lasting protection, because trypanosomes keep changing their outer coat and there are several species. A recovered donkey can be infected again if it goes back to fly-infested areas. There is currently no vaccine, so fly control, careful grazing and vet-advised preventive treatment are the main protection.

faqs.q: Can a donkey with trypanosomiasis infect my cattle?
faqs.a: The donkey does not pass it directly by touching other animals, but flies that bite a sick donkey can carry parasites to cattle, goats and camels nearby, and cattle can infect donkeys the same way. If one animal is diagnosed, ask your vet to check the rest of the herd and step up fly control for all animals.

faqs.q: Should I keep my donkey working lightly while it is being treated?
faqs.a: No. A donkey with trypanosomiasis is anaemic, so its blood carries less oxygen, and work can make it collapse or slow recovery. Rest it fully until the vet says it can start light work again, and build up workload gradually as weight and strength return.

products.role: An oral rehydration and heat-stress relief solution that can be offered in drinking water to help a feverish, weak donkey stay hydrated and keep drinking during illness and recovery. It supports the animal alongside vet-prescribed trypanocide treatment, rest and fly control; it does not kill trypanosomes or treat the disease.

card.headline: Swollen lumps under the jaw
card.look: The donkey is dull, off its feed and has thick yellow pus running from the nose. Hot, painful swellings appear under the jaw or behind the cheek, and some burst and drain pus.
card.action: Separate the sick donkey from all other donkeys, horses and mules at once, give it its own water bucket, and call your vet.

aka: Bastard strangles (when abscesses spread inside the body)
detail.summary: Strangles is a highly contagious bacterial infection of the nose, throat and lymph nodes of donkeys, horses and mules. Lymph nodes are small glands that filter germs; in strangles they swell and fill with pus. The disease gets its name because badly swollen glands can squeeze the throat and make breathing hard. Most donkeys recover with good nursing and vet care, but it spreads fast through yards, markets and watering points, keeps working donkeys off work for weeks, and can cause serious complications.
detail.cause: Strangles is caused by the bacterium Streptococcus equi subspecies equi. It enters through the nose or mouth and settles in the lining of the nose and throat. Within days it moves into the lymph nodes under the jaw and around the throat, where the body fights it and pus builds up. The glands become hot, swollen and painful, and they often burst on the outside or drain into the throat. Some pus drains into the guttural pouches, two air-filled sacs at the back of the head found only in equines. Pus left there can harden into small balls called chondroids, and the bacteria can hide in them for months or even years. A donkey like this may look healthy but still spread the disease; it is called a carrier. Occasionally the bacteria travel through the blood to other organs such as the lungs, liver or gut, forming hidden abscesses. In a few animals the immune system over-reacts and damages small blood vessels, a condition called purpura haemorrhagica. Other respiratory infections in donkeys, such as equine influenza, equine herpesvirus and bacterial pneumonia, can look similar and often hit when animals are stressed, overworked, cold or crowded.
spread: Direct nose-to-nose contact between donkeys, horses and mules, especially when animals meet at markets, shared grazing or watering points.
Shared water troughs, buckets and feed troughs contaminated with nasal discharge or pus; the bacteria can survive for some time in water and on damp surfaces.
Shared equipment such as halters, bits, harnesses, cart shafts, grooming brushes and nose bags.
People's hands, clothes and shoes after handling a sick donkey, then moving on to healthy animals.
Carrier donkeys that have recovered or never looked very sick but still shed bacteria from the guttural pouches, often bringing the disease into a new herd after purchase.
Bursting abscesses, which release large amounts of infectious pus onto the ground, walls and bedding.
Stress from heavy work, long journeys, poor feeding and cold wet weather, which lowers resistance and makes outbreaks worse.
detail.atRisk: Young donkeys, especially foals after weaning and animals under about five years, are most at risk because they have not yet built immunity. Very old, thin, overworked or poorly fed donkeys also suffer more. Any donkey that mixes with others is at risk, so the danger is highest in working donkeys that pull carts in towns, carry water to shared boreholes and dams, or are taken to livestock markets. Newly bought animals and herds that receive new arrivals without a quarantine period are common sources of outbreaks. In pastoral areas, donkeys that gather at shared water points during the dry season mix closely, while the cold, wet long and short rains add stress and crowding in shelters. Donkeys kept near horses, for example on farms, schools or tourist sites, can pass infection both ways. Donkeys are stoic animals that hide pain and illness, so they are often sicker than they look by the time the farmer notices.

early: Fever: the donkey feels hot, and a thermometer in the rectum reads above the normal range, often noticeably high; fever may appear a day or two before any discharge.
Dullness, standing quietly with head low, ears back and less interest in surroundings; in donkeys this quiet behaviour is easy to miss.
Eating less or eating slowly, dropping food or reluctance to swallow because the throat is sore.
A clear, watery nasal discharge that quickly turns thick, creamy and yellow.
A soft cough, often worse when the donkey eats or moves.
Warm, tender swelling starting under the jaw between the two jawbones or just behind the cheek.
advanced: Large, hard and very painful swellings under the jaw or behind the ear that later soften and burst, releasing thick yellow pus.
Holding the head and neck stretched out stiffly to ease pain, and avoiding lowering the head to eat or drink.
Noisy, rough or difficult breathing, sometimes with a snoring or whistling sound, because swollen glands press on the airway; this is an emergency.
Food and water coming back out through the nose because swallowing is painful or blocked.
Weight loss and weakness after days of poor eating, with sunken eyes and dry gums from dehydration.
Swelling of the legs, belly or head and tiny red or purple spots on the gums or inside the eyelids, which can signal purpura haemorrhagica.
Ongoing fever, colic (belly pain), weight loss or lumps in new places weeks after apparent recovery, which may mean abscesses have spread inside the body.

lookalikes.name: Equine influenza or equine herpesvirus (viral respiratory infection)
lookalikes.howToTell: Viral infections usually cause a sudden high fever, a frequent dry cough and watery discharge that may turn cloudy, often spreading very fast through the whole group. Big pus-filled abscesses under the jaw are not typical. A vet needs swabs to be sure, and antibiotics do not cure these viruses.

lookalikes.name: Lungworm (Dictyocaulus arnfieldi)
lookalikes.howToTell: Donkeys often carry lungworm with few signs, but some develop a long-lasting cough without high fever or jaw swellings. The cough persists for weeks and improves after vet-advised deworming. Donkeys carrying lungworm can infect horses grazing with them.

lookalikes.name: Tooth root abscess or sinus infection
lookalikes.howToTell: Discharge usually comes from one nostril only, is often foul-smelling, and the donkey may have a swelling on the face or jaw bone, bad breath or chewing problems. It does not spread to other donkeys, and there is often no fever.

lookalikes.name: African horse sickness or glanders (notifiable diseases)
lookalikes.howToTell: African horse sickness causes high fever, swelling around the eyes and head, frothy nasal discharge and severe breathing difficulty, often during or after the rains when biting midges are active. Glanders causes nodules and ulcers inside the nose and along the legs. Both are legally notifiable in Kenya and glanders can infect people, so if you see these signs report to the County Veterinary Officer immediately.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually suspects strangles from the signs: fever, thick yellow nasal discharge and swollen glands under the jaw, especially when several equines are affected. To confirm it, the vet takes a swab from the nose or throat, or draws pus from an abscess with a needle, and sends it to a laboratory for culture (growing the bacteria) or PCR (a test that detects the bacteria's genetic material). Some referral centres can look inside the guttural pouches with an endoscope, a thin camera tube, and wash them out to find carriers; this is not widely available in Kenya, so your vet will advise what is realistic. Blood tests can show whether a donkey has been exposed recently and help decide on vaccination or screening. The vet will also listen to the chest to check for pneumonia and look for signs of complications. Before the vet arrives, write down when each animal first got sick, their temperatures if you have a thermometer, how much each is eating and drinking, any recent purchases, journeys, markets or contact with other equines, and any medicines already given. Keep the sick donkey in a place where the vet can examine it safely.
firstSteps: Isolate the sick donkey straight away in a separate shelter or paddock away from other donkeys, horses and mules, ideally where they cannot touch noses or share a fence line.
Give the sick donkey its own water bucket, feed trough, halter and grooming tools, and do not share them with any other animal until the vet says it is safe.
Stop all work and travel for the sick donkey and for any in-contact equines, and do not take any of them to market, shared water points or grazing with neighbours' animals.
Offer clean, fresh water at all times and soft, moist food that is easy to swallow, such as soaked hay, soaked bran or fresh tender grass, placed at a height the donkey can reach comfortably.
Keep the donkey dry, sheltered from cold rain and wind, and shaded from hot sun, with clean, dry bedding.
Do not squeeze, cut or burst the swellings yourself; the vet may advise warm compresses to help them mature and will decide when to open them.
Watch the breathing closely, and call the vet as an emergency if the donkey breathes noisily, struggles for air, or stops eating and drinking completely.

Look after the healthy animals first and the sick one last, wash your hands with soap afterwards, and change or wash clothes and footwear; check the temperature of in-contact donkeys daily if you can and isolate any that develop fever.
detail.vetTreatment: Most donkeys with strangles are treated mainly with good nursing and supportive care, while the immune system clears the infection. The vet may lance (cut open) a mature, soft abscess under hygienic conditions so pus can drain, and then flush it with a dilute antiseptic; the pus must be collected and disposed of carefully because it is highly infectious. Anti-inflammatory painkillers from the NSAID group, such as flunixin or phenylbutazone, may be prescribed to reduce fever and throat pain so the donkey eats and drinks again. Donkeys process many drugs differently from horses, so medicines and plans designed for horses must be adjusted by a vet. Antibiotics are a careful decision: penicillin is the usual choice for Streptococcus equi, and it may be used in very early cases, in animals with breathing problems, or when abscesses spread inside the body. In a donkey that already has abscesses forming, antibiotics can delay them maturing, prolong the illness and interfere with natural immunity, so the vet may advise against them. Never buy antibiotics from an agrovet and use them without a vet's prescription; wrong or incomplete courses help bacteria become resistant (antimicrobial resistance), making future infections harder to treat. Severe cases with airway blockage may need emergency procedures, and purpura haemorrhagica needs urgent and specialised treatment. If any medicine is given, follow the vet's withdrawal period before milk from the jenny is used or the animal is slaughtered. Expect the course of illness to last from a couple of weeks to over a month, with follow-up visits and possibly testing before the donkey rejoins the herd.
prevention: Quarantine every newly bought or returning donkey, horse or mule for at least two to three weeks, away from your other animals, and check its temperature daily; ask your vet about testing new animals before they join the herd.
Buy donkeys from known, healthy sources, and avoid animals with nasal discharge, cough or lumps under the jaw, or from yards with a recent outbreak.
Use separate water buckets and feed troughs for each animal where possible, and avoid letting your donkeys drink from shared troughs at markets or public water points during an outbreak.
Do not share halters, bits, harnesses, nose bags or brushes between donkeys, and clean and disinfect equipment regularly, especially after any illness.
After an outbreak, remove bedding and manure, scrub shelters, buckets and troughs with detergent then disinfectant, and let them dry in the sun before reuse.
Keep recovered donkeys isolated until your vet advises they are no longer shedding the bacteria, since some become long-term carriers.
Feed donkeys well with good roughage, clean water, salt or mineral licks, and allow proper rest between work, because a well-nourished, unstressed donkey resists infection better.

Provide a dry, well-ventilated shelter with protection from cold rain and wind, deworm on a vet-advised plan that covers lungworm, and ask your vet whether a strangles vaccine is available and suitable, as access in Kenya is limited.
detail.impact: For many Kenyan families a donkey is a source of daily income, carrying water, firewood, farm produce and building materials, or pulling carts for hire. A donkey with strangles must rest for several weeks, and so should in-contact animals, so that income stops and families may have to pay for water or transport. Vet visits, drugs and extra feed add costs. Because the disease spreads so easily, a single sick donkey bought at market can infect every equine on a farm or in a village. Thin, overworked donkeys lose further condition and may take a long time to return to full work. Deaths are not common, but complications such as airway blockage, spread of abscesses inside the body or purpura haemorrhagica can be fatal or cause long-term ill health. Carrier animals can keep outbreaks going year after year, and jennies used for milking lose production while sick.
detail.humanHealth: Strangles bacteria very rarely infect people, but a few cases have been reported, mostly in people with weak immune systems. A related bacterium that can cause respiratory infections in donkeys, Streptococcus zooepidemicus, has occasionally caused serious illness in people, including through drinking unpasteurised milk. Glanders, which can look similar, is dangerous to humans. Wear gloves when handling pus or cleaning discharge, wash your hands well with soap and water, keep children away from sick animals, and do not drink raw milk from a sick jenny. Boil any donkey milk before use, and respect the vet's withdrawal period for milk and meat after any treatment.
detail.outlook: Most donkeys recover from strangles with good nursing, isolation and vet care, usually over two to six weeks once the abscesses have drained. Recovery is faster in young adults that are well fed and rested, and slower in foals, old, thin or overworked animals. Many recovered donkeys have good protection for some time, but immunity is not guaranteed for life and some animals can be infected again. The outlook is worse if the donkey develops breathing difficulty, pneumonia, abscesses inside the body or purpura haemorrhagica, so early vet involvement matters. Some recovered donkeys remain carriers without looking sick, which is why follow-up and continued hygiene are important even after the herd looks healthy.

faqs.q: Can my donkey give strangles to my horse or mule?
faqs.a: Yes. Strangles spreads easily between donkeys, horses and mules in both directions. Keep a sick donkey well away from all other equines, do not share water or equipment, and handle the sick animal last. Tell neighbours who keep equines so they can protect their animals too.

faqs.q: Can I keep working my donkey if it only has a small runny nose?
faqs.a: No. A donkey with fever, nasal discharge or a swollen throat should rest completely. Work makes the illness worse, slows recovery and spreads the bacteria to other donkeys at water points, markets and on the road. Check its temperature, isolate it and ask your vet when it is safe to return to work.

faqs.q: Should I buy antibiotics from the agrovet and inject my donkey myself?
faqs.a: Please do not. In strangles, antibiotics given at the wrong time can delay abscesses maturing, make the illness last longer and stop the donkey building its own immunity. Using them without a vet's prescription also drives antibiotic resistance. Donkeys also handle many drugs differently from horses, so only a vet should decide on any medicine, the right product and how it is given.

faqs.q: Should I burst the swelling under the jaw?
faqs.a: No. Squeezing or cutting the swelling yourself is painful for the donkey, can cause infection to spread and releases highly infectious pus where other animals and people can pick it up. Your vet may advise warm compresses to help it soften, and will open it hygienically when it is ready.

faqs.q: How long must the sick donkey stay away from the others?
faqs.a: Usually for several weeks after the last signs have gone, not just until it looks well. Some donkeys keep shedding the bacteria long after recovery. Your vet will advise how long to isolate and whether testing is possible to check the donkey is no longer infectious before it rejoins the group.

faqs.q: My donkey had strangles last year and is fine now, so why did the disease come back to my herd?
faqs.a: Some recovered donkeys become carriers, with bacteria hiding in the guttural pouches at the back of the head. They look healthy but can shed the bacteria from time to time, especially when stressed. New animals bought without quarantine are another common source. Talk to your vet about screening, keep up good hygiene and always quarantine new arrivals.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that can be offered in drinking water to a sick donkey that is still drinking, to help replace fluids and salts lost through fever and poor intake and to encourage it to keep drinking while it recovers. It supports hydration only, does not treat the infection, and should be used alongside vet care and good nursing; never force or drench fluids into a donkey that is struggling to swallow, as it may choke.
